title: Wichita Indians
description:
Wichita Indians

At the Carlisle school many photographs were taken of groups of Indian students. We did not think that similar photos were taken of Lincoln Institution Indian students, but recently we came across the following photo of 11 Wichita boys.

The boys are: top row: Wah-kish (Edward Moore); Jeks (Chester Collins); Indian name unknown (Philip Hendrix); Indian name unknown (Hall Stevenson); Ne-do (James Ross). Middle row: Indian name unknown (Charles Ross); Ohdo (Ray Hendrix); Indian name unknown (Oliver Standing); Do-dits-se-ah (William Luther), Indian name unknown (Roland Stevenson). Bottom row: Indian name unknown (Lynn Casard).

The photo was taken between 1887 and 1892, which was the period that most of the boys attended the Lincoln Institution.

children.text:
Luther Standing Bear was a Sioux Indian, and the son of a chief, who had heard of the Indian School being set up in Carlisle. So, he made his way to Carlisle only to find there was nobody there as Richard Pratt, the director, was away trying recruit Indians for the school. He was thereby the first pupil at Carlisle and he became a prized pupil. When the Wanamakers requested 2 Indians to come and work at their store in center-city Philadelphia, he was the first choice.

While he was working at Wanamakers he lived in the Educational Home. There he witnessed the first efforts of Mary McHenry Cox to bring Indian boys to the Lincoln Institution school. At the weekends he would join with the other Indians at the Home in their singing and music-making. 

Luther wanted to stay on at Wanamakers but not to live at the Educational Home. He could not find anyone who was willing to provide board for him in Philadelphia. In the end he returned to Carlisle and then his Reservation, where he started his career, which included being part of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West Show and acting in movies.

title: Chapter 1 In the Beginning, 1681 - 1704
newspaper: Easttown, Old in History, Young in Spirit, 1704 - 2004 by C. Herbert Fry

children.text:
Chapter 1: In the Beginning

1681 - 1704

On September 15th, 1681 some Welshmen of means purchased 40,000 or 50,000 acres from William Penn (commonly known as the “Welsh Tract”).

{incorrect, it was not a purchase, it was an agreement that the area could be purchased by Welsh Quakers where they could have their own language and customs. It should also be noted that this was a verbal agreement (as were a lot of Penn’s early land sales)}

It was to have been in land lying contiguous, subject to local government of the Welsh Friends to whom the land was apportioned.

It included Haverford, Merion, Radnor, Tredyffrin, and subsequently the greater part of Newtown, Goshen, and Uwchland townships, for Penn was unable to redeem all of his promises of a separate colony or Welsh “barony.” This caused great dissatisfaction, especially after the division of counties cut the Welsh Quaker settlements in two, and they found themselves in a minority. Politically it probably kept some very able men out of office, but gave the death blow to a clan of citizens perpetuating a dialect, for the Welsh had dwelt for ages in proximity to the Englsh and yet preserved their own peculiar language, a language that was forgotten in America in less than three generations.

Wales was not and never had been a rich country. The people were poor, proud, and found it difficult to forgive a slight upon their dignity, but there are degrees of poverty, for some were not so poor that they were under the necessity of engaging in business, the so-called landed gentry. Yet they held that a man might follow any honorable calling or trade and remain a gentleman.

The prime motive that induced the Welshman to give up the impoverished land was to better his condition economically. Wales, too, was in the midst of religious dissentions and many non-conformists suffered persecution from the Established Church and longed to be free of religious conflicts.

Penn’s terms were liberal, 100 pounds sterling for 5000 acres, subject to a quit rent of one shilling for every 100 acres, payable upon the first day of March, forever; which last clause became a dead letter following the Revolution. Many were content to purchase 500 acres or less, and the more affluent were attended by numerous kinsmen, ostensibly as servants, anxious to partake in Penn’s bounty of 50 acres for each, and his guarantee of religious freedom.

Thus the early Welshmen flocked to the western shore of the Delaware. A sturdy, worthy people, more clannish and old fashioned than the English, Dutch, and Swedes who had proceeded them here, but they were the best in Wales. The women is tall beaver hats and outlandish cloaks, were good wives and mothers. They came to brighten up the waste places in the New World. Their fate, however, was not only to toil from sunrise to sunset, but by candle or fire light at night, and their joy to add the feminine touch to the home, to plant the flower garden in the few moments of leisure, and to initiate the young in the rudiments of book knowledge, often with the Bible as the only text book.

Like all other races, the Welsh brought with them all the prejudice of the old country, and the petty differences of crred continued to separate neighbors. Settlers living convenient to a meeting house not of their own persuasion underwent considerable hardship over the rough roads to the house of their own peculiar denomonation.

Although not included in the Welsh “barony,” Easttown did have 100 acres surveyed to Welsh settlers by its First Purchasers. Easttown originally was entirely in the possessionof three Englsih land speculators. Interestingly, the Easttown Welsh were Church of England men, not Quakers.

William Wood and William Sharlow, the latter a prosperous London merchant, appear to have been the so called “First Purchasers” of part of northern Easttown. James Claypoole, a friend of Penn’s, a member of the Free Society of Traders and the first prothonotary of Philadelphia, received a grant for a block of 1050 acres extending across the southwest part. These men were non-residents of Easttown although it is possible that Claypoole had someone is his employ clear off some ground near the present location of Leopard. Newtown “Street” was laid out north from Newtown to near the Easttown border in 1683.

{See the Easttown deed history here, which contradicts some of the statements in this section.}

The Welsh tract in Easttown made up less than 20% of the total township land. It was bounded on the west by the line of Newtown Street road north to what is today the Tredyffrin line. The eastern boundary passed from the corner of today’s Conestoga and Berwyn Baptist roads south across Lancaster avenue and down the little valley of the branch of Darby creek through the western partof Devon back to the border of Newtown. When in 1691 a deed was made by an heir of William Wood to Howell James for “a tract containing 500 acres on the upper end of Newtown,” a preliminary step had been taken in the history of Easttown.

“East Town” as it was originally written, was so called from its position in the county. Settlement was not rpurred by any outstanding resources, waterways, mineral assets or unusually fertile soil. Locations of early saw mills indicate that some of its terrain was covered with forests.A natural feature influencing the land was the many meandering tributaries of Darby creek.

The date assigned to formation of Easttown is 1704. It is first mentioned on the court records by the appointment of William Thomas as its constable, on December 27, 1704. The resident land owners in 1715 were Edward, Ellis, Owen and Morgan Hugh, Philip and John David, David Davis and John Harris, Hugh Jones, Evan Thomas, Richard Evans, and Thomas Edwards, all from Wales and nearly all Friends or Episcopalians. There were 21 taxable settlers in 1730, 25 in 1740, 39 in 1750, and 51 in 1760.

Tradition informs us that a blockhouse for defense against the Indians was erected on an Indian clearing in the northwest angle of Sugartown and Newtown roads, just south of Berwyn, and that the first religious services, some 15 or 20 years before St. David's Church was built, were held there. This clearing was also used by the early settlers as a burial ground.

The first known settlement on land in Easttown took place between 1703 and 1706 at what became know as Travelgwyn. The exact meaning or significance of the name is obscure, but it can be translated as "white toil or trouble." The most ancient deed to the Travelgwyn estate was in Welsh, which had to be produced and translated before the Ivesters could complete a more recent sale.

This tract is just south of Berwyn, on either side of Waterloo avenue and near the foot of Waters’ Hill, and is described in a lengthy deed dated December 4, 1706. 

The tract contained the original log cabin which has been described as a single-storied structure with double-pitched roof, one window and the door in front and a single window in the rear. It was possibly of two rooms, had a large open fireplace, and was situated east of the present stone farmhouse and near to a spring of water on the old Ivester farm, the cabin being last used as a chicken house. At this period Trav-el-gwyn was mostly in timber, the swamp a covert for woodcock, and the branch of the Darby creek swarmed with speckled trout. It was passed on in the family fifteen years later.

The foregoing owners were closely connected, Edward Hughs being a brother to Philip Davies’ wife and Evan Hughs a nephew of the last and son of Edward Hughs, former owner. Philip Davies evidently built the stone house sometime between 1706 and 1722.

On February 20, 1723, this estate was sold by Evan and Ann Hughes, of Easttown, to Griffith Hughes, clerk of Radnor, for 140 pounds. Here it is called Grove Hall, formerly Travelgwyn. The deed was signed by Evan Hughes and the mark of his wife Ann.

The Rev. Griffith Hughes graduated from Oxford in 1732, and was appointed rector of Radnor and Perkiomen (St. David’s and St. James’ Episcopal Churches), but here we find that he was in Radnor and Easttown at least ten years earlier as a clerk and doubtless a student under Rev. Weyman and Rev. Backhouse at St. David’s.

On August 2, 1735, “being the Eight Year of the reign of King George the second,” Griffith Hugh, Clerk, secured a mortgage loan of 95 pounds, 4 shillings from Mordecai Lewis of New Town. The mortgage land description is the first attempt to set forth the one hundred-acre tract by metes and bounds and the first mention of the old graveyard.

On February 13, 1743, by an indenture “Between Griffith Hughs, late of Easttown but now Rector of St. Lucy’s in the Island of Barbados, and John Hughs of Mirian in the County of Philadelphia, Yeoman, Attorney of the said Griffith Hughs Legally Constituted of the one part and Griffith James of Easttown afforsd, Yeoman, of the other part,” Griffith James came into possession of Grove Hall, or Travelgwyn, for the sum of 120 pounds and here he lived for over twenty years.

There is a tradition that his daughter Hannah in her girlhood planted an acorn in the southeast corner of the yard of that which is now known as the Waters’ place, from which grew the great white oak over two hundred fifty years old when it fell on March 24, 1996.

When Griffith James died he left a will dated August 24, 1764 which transferred the property to his wife Ann.

Ann James died October 27, 1773 leaving daughter Hannah sole heir of Grove Hall. Hannah married Whitehead Wetherby a son of Benjamin Wetherby, who was brother-in-law of Dr. Barnado Van Leer of Marple and one time innkeeper at the old Blue Ball Tavern on the Conestoga road.

There was little excitement or romance in the settlement of Easttown for the Indians were few and peaceable. Early in Colonial times the native families were settled upon small reservations: the Okehockings on about 500 acres in lower Willistown along the Ridley creek, another along the Brandywine; reservations that were respected but a little while by the white man. Indeed the Indian left so slight an impression upon our township that not a single native geographical name is in use today.

Both Penn and the early colonists have left some account of the so-called “Indian clearings” and the mulberry and peach trees growing thereon. However, not all are satisfied that these orchards originated with the Indians. While the red mulberry is a native of America, the peach is said to have been indigenous in Persia. It is possible that these orchards were planted with seed brought over by some of the earlier Swedish or Dutch fur traders.

While there was little need of fighting men in the early settlements, there was a great demand for able-bodied men skilled in swinging the ax and in clearing the ground. Penn recommended clearing 15 acres the first year and building a log house 18 x 30 feet, with a partition through the middle and another to divide one end in two smaller rooms, and with a loft over all with a floor of clapboards, and the ground floor of earth.

The forest, mostly deciduous, with more or less pine on the hills, was a century or more old. As it had been long the custom of the Indians to fire the fallen leaves and brush to facilitate the hunting of game, it was usually free of undergrowth and open enough to drive a horse and a light cart in many places.

The Old Lancaster (Conestoga) road, or the King’s highway as it was officially known, followed more or less faithfully an old Indian trail to the mouth of the Schuylkill, for the natives in traversing the backbone of the watershed between the Schuylkill and Delaware, followed the ridge, the path of least resistance. It was the first road, and is said to have been surveyed in 1700 from Philadelphia to the Susquehanna near the mouth of the Conestoga creek, though it was not completed until 1741.

The Provincial Council took the necessary action May 27, 1718, to lay out a road from the Brandywine to the Conestoga. On November 23, 1721, relative to dispute in parallel roads: “It is Ordered that the Road now and heretofore used leading from Philadelphia to Conestogoe, through the Townships of Meirion and Radnor, and laid out by the authority of this Government as far as Thomas Moore’s Mill (Downingtown) on the Brandy Wine River or Creek, be deemed the King’s Highway and public Road.”

They spelled road in those days with a capital “R”, but apparently the exact lines were still a matter of doubt or dispute, since on October 4, 1733, the commissioners appointed January 29, 1730/31 to lay out the road to Lancaster made report that they found it inadvisable to discover where it had been altered while the corn crop was growing, and it continued in an unsettled state until July 20, 1741, when a survey over the entire route was submitted and approved by Council.

It included the more than four miles through Tredyffrin and 292 feet in “East Town”, from the Willistown line to the upper line of Radnor, with 23 angles, and mentions the “Sign of the Ball,” or Blue Ball tavern.

Gulf road was a line of communication as early as 1690, though not officially laid out until 1748, and the Swedesford, in the valley, and the Darby, Newtown, and Sugartown roads were in place in 1700 substantially as today.

Chapter 3: Pre-Revolutionary Period

1761 - 1774

The clearing of the wilderness proved too great a task for the Welsh unaided. Great tracts in this community remained untouched. Many of the younger generation sought less strenuous labor. In comparison with the Scotch-Irish, the ideal pioneers of America, the Welsh were more clever and as stubborn in argument as the former were in a fight; but neither the average Welshman nor the typical North of Ireland man were born farmers.

Many of the Welsh were land poor, since the French and Indian wars had increased the taxes and at the same time encouraged the German emigrants and redemptioners to settle throughout the area, from about 1763 to the beginning of the Revolution. The German invasion of this region, like that of the Scotch-Irish, apparently had its inception more on economic than religious grounds.

Many of these tracts lay some distance from the public roads, hence lane or land rights, also water rights, were freely granted. The movement resulted in two or three practically continuous German settlements in the eastern, central, and western parts of the territory extending substantially across the cultivated land. 

That the Germans settled in such numbers as to seriously dispute with the Welsh the language of the community is a matter of doubt. The dream of a Welsh barony had dissipated long since and the Cymric dialect, present only in the earlier records of the religious bodies, had died with the second generation. All legal documents, gravestones, etc., were in English. The English and Scotch spoke no other than English; the Welsh after the first generation understood it, and the Germans had to learn it.

Jacob Frick, of Swiss origin, arrived in America according to the family records in September of 1733 and settled first near Pottstown. About 1740 he married Elizabeth Urner who died in 1757 shortly after the birth of their youngest son, John. It is believed that the Frick family attended Coventry German Baptist Brethren Church. John was reared by Catharine (previous surname unknown) Frick, who was Jacob's second wife.

In 1769, when John was 12 years old, the family moved to a 100-acre farm located in the Chester valley of Tredyffrin township “two miles from Valley Forge,” where they lived during the Revolution, “near the scene of the Paoli massacre, and where the British and Hessian army encamped after the battle of Brandywine.” John was assigned to the Tredyffrin militia, but, as a German Baptist, he did not attend meetings and was fined. Jacob Frick does not appear on the tax list of 1771, but he is listed for 100 acres, two horses, and two cows in 1774 and in subsequent years. The place was located at what a century later was the Abraham farm at New Centerville. John Frick reported a loss of £120 due to depradations during the British encampment in 1777.

The farm “descended” to Nathaniel and Christiana Frick Jones. Christiana was John’s half-sister, as she was the first child of Jacob Frick’s second marriage. The Jones farm was located adjacent to the Frick farm.

The early tax collectors. often illiterate, seldom recorded the occupations of the taxpayers until about a decade prior to the Revolution. Then it appeared that not only nearly all the German emigrants had some trade or another, but that there was quite a sprinkling of the second or third generation of the original settlers with occupations other than that of farmer or farm laborer. However, all or nearly all, including the preachers managed farms of greater or lesser extent. 

John Davis and, later, James Currie, of Tredyffrin, are recorded as physicians; Sampson Davis kept the store at Spread Eagle in 1766 and he was followed by Richard Miles. Christian Workizer had a shop near Howell’s tavern, and Samuel Davis had a store near by, probably at Paoli.

Isaac and Anthony Wayne operated a tanyard at their farm “Waynesborough” and doubtless supplied oak and hemlock tanned cowhide to the cordwainers, or shoemakers, of the vicinity - Amos Jones, John Briggs, Daniel James, John Keck and Boston Rink. The latter took care of the custom of “Cockletown.” Morris Morris, Thomas Jones, and Thomas Williams looked after the footwear and probably the saddles and harness of Easttown.

Benjamin Robinson, followed by Mathias Woolman, were weavers of this period, soon reinforced by James Nealy (Cockletown), John Baker, Henry Ruth, Peter Stickler, Peter Stedler (Spread Eagle), Daniel and Felty Shewalter, with Christian Brannaman (“Brandyman”), Henry McQuead and John Fulton of Easttown. There were many ways of spellinng the Neely family name. which appear on these pages are an accurate representation of the many variations found in documents of the 18th and 19th centries. For example, it is splet two different ways in th title of a 1795 court petition.

James Davis (1767) and John Dunbar (1768 - 1769) were assessed for a fulling mill, probably the same one, and William Bailey is listed as a fuller (one who bleaches or whitens wool or cloth). 

There were blacksmith shops in the vicinity of the Spread Eagle, Paoli, Howell’s, and the Leopard at a very early date. Later, David, a son of William Evans, the first blacksmith at Paoli, ran a shop in addition to a hundred acre farm. Paul Sharraden (1769 - 1774) and Joel WattsJoshua Evans , Spread Eagle, Thomas Pennington, Howell’s tavern and Morris Davis also followed the blacksmith trade. Joseph Massey, Anthony Thomas, and Thomas Watkins ran the Easttown shops.

Joshua Evans was a carpenter until he turned to tavern keeping and politics at Paoli. Humphrey Wain is listed as a “joyner”; Robert Fullerton, painter; William Pomroy, tinsman; Robert McGuigan (Easttown), butcher; Joshua Humphreys, clockmaker; Peter Mather (later taven keeper at the Warren), vendue cryer; and Benjamin Ronbinson, lemon peddler.

Perhaps there is no business more simple and lucrative than that of distilling spirits. This became clear during the first few years of the Prohibition. In the early history of the country the distillation of strong drink was one of the first industries engaged in as an honorable employment and there were many unrecorded stills for rye whiskey. One was located on the Davis farm just below Howell’s tavern, another at the “Black Swan” in the wooded ravine below Neeley’s and another just back of Neeley’s on the hillside.

The Neeley log cabin still stands on Old State road one block north of T/E Middle School and is used as a residence today.

Swift flowing water is needed to power a mill. Easttown has but a short stretch of the Darby creek of sufficient the emigrant, came from Merionethshire, Wales, 1708, with his wife Jean and son John. Ellis Pugh also came on the same ship and taught young John his ABC's on shipboard. John Morris' grandson, Lewis, came from Hilltown, Bucks County to Easttown in 1764 and bought land, some of which is still in this family.

Sometime during the late colonial or pre-Revolutionary period a straggling hamlet of less than a score of humble homes came to be known as Cockletown. It extended for half a mile or more along the Lancaster, later known as the Conestoga or Old road; from a short distance in Easttown east of the Fox tavern (Francis avenue), to a little beyond Peggy’s corner (Howellville road) in Tredyffrin; and flourished up to the Turnpike era.

Although situated on the first and chief inland highway of the province, it was somewhat isolated locally. The nearest crossroads, the Welsh Line or Baptist road, was a mile to the east and the Bear road a mile and a half to the west.

There then existed, however, a private wood road or right of way, through the Atkinson, later John Reese land, leading down to the valley and on out to the Swedesford road (today’s Circuit City store) near Wilson’s Corner.

Another bypath began at Peggy’s Corner, which gave access to the Neilley’s and continued down the wooded ravine to the Black Swan distillery and beyond through the Reese plantation, with several gates, to the Swedesford road opposite the present entrance to Chesterbrook.

A third ancient lane, a quarter of a mile west of Peggy’s Corner, entered deeply in the hills and turned to a dead end in Prissy’s bottom (where today’s Bodine road turns uphill to the south), giving access to the residents of some five or six log houses on the southern exposure of the hills; but this right of way extended no further, except by footpath, to Howell’s Tavern, now Howellville. 

Scarcely more than a hundred yards north of the Old road at any point and sometimes bordering it, was an almost unbroken forest of deciduous timber, with here and there a stand of pitch pine, and frequently a dense border of red cedar. The hills and ravines of the Slate ridge, or South Valley hills, had also a dense under growth of laurel and wild grape vine; the small bogs or swamps an almost impenetrable mass of spicewood and green-brier.

The dwellings of this early settlement at Cockletown, perhaps the earliest incipient town of Easttown, were mostly of the log cabin type, built of oak or chestnut logs, with stone chimneys; occasionally one more pretentious had stout stone gable ends. However, they were mostly small and homely, erected so close to the right of way that the habitants could step from the doorsill directly into the road. On one side was the wood pile and the well with its windlass and oaken bucket; on the other the lye barrel, the lilac bush, the clump of hollyhocks, and more than likely the pig pen.

Few of these squatters, tenants or small land owners kept a horse; but few were without a cow, at least two hogs, and a flock of poultry.

The cleared plots were not extensive, though ample to grow enough corn, potatoes, cabbage, turnips, and pumpkins to carry the stock and family over the winter. They planted five grains of corn to the hill, according to the proverb:

One for the blackbird one for the crow;
one to rot, and two to grow.

However remote from town, Cockletown was by no means lonely. Until about 1730 the Old road had been almost exclusively a packhorse trail, as it had been more anciently an Indian path. Later it became a thoroughfare fifty feet wide for traders, emigrants, drovers, freighters in Conestoga wagons, etc., deep in mire or dust, according to the season or state of the weather, and the small homesteader could no longer plant his corn in the middle of the road and require the occasional traveler to detour as best he could.

This hamlet, was only locally known at Cockletown., but whether given in honor of the alleged ancient Welsh national flower, the corn cockle, as some say, or in disrespect by the more prosperous farmers, who centrainly regarded the hill clearings as “fit only for growing timber and weeds,” is an open question.

In the Burn family papers there is the statement of Eizabeth Burn, nee Jones, who was born in 1797, four miles east of this place and an actuak resident here from 1832 to 1879. She asserted that this place was called Cockletown and that the name was derived from the cornflower, an imported European weeed closely related to the ragged robin, which flourished and became very troublesome in the wheat fields.

The settlers at first had no other means of lighting their cabins than that furnished by the open fireplace, but after awhile they became more affluent and tallow dips came in fashion.

Well dressed, notched and chinked log dwellings, though snug and warm, had one great fault. The American bug indigenous to the inner bark of the anceient hemlock, frequently transferred to the log cabin and was difficult to eradicate. This condition of affairs gave expression to a none too polite or delicate saying: 

Good night! Sleep tight! Don’t let the bugs bite!

Proceeding westward on the Old Lancaster road in Easttown, there were two small log houses on the north side, one in front of where Westley Jones, shoemaker, built his new frame house in 1862, and the other close to the entrance to the late Dr. Okie’s place. On the south side there was at least one, possibly two, log dwellings.

This land was a small part of the 2000 acre tract patented by William Wood and William Sharlow, surveyed August 21,1684, and in the sub-division of l000 acres of the latter, November 28, 1704. The entire tract then came into the possession of Richard Harrison, and later, September 11, 1746, Samuel Harrison, and 119 acres, later to Standish Ford.,

Then came the Fox tavern, the only building entirely of stone. Its erection is of unknown date. Historian Julius Sachse informs us that it was kept by Fox from 1792 to 1797, and by David Llewellyn until 1804, when it ceased to be a place of public entertainment and became a country store.

Its site marked the extreme northeastern corner of the l000 acre “Travelgwyn” tract of William Wood. The northern quarter section of 250 acres came into the possession of ten persons in succession, the last being Peter Elliot, April 15, 1723.

The old tavern was demolished about 1900 by the late Joseph Williams family to make way for a more modern dwelling. Old English coins have been found while digging in the vicinity, probably relics of the pitch-penny period.

The next tract on the south side of the road is also mostly in Easttown and early belonged to Peter Elliot who was a blacksmith.

The early Tredyffrin ownership of the land on which Cockletown was situated, appears less complicated than that of the Easttown end. William Standly patented 300 acres between the two Welsh lines, Baptist road and the Welsh line near Peggy’s Corner. This was a strip immediately north of the Easttown line. Its entire acreage was acquired by John Day and passed to his widow Hannah (her second husband was James Atkinson) and then to Grace Peadwell, Hannah’s daughter. Thomas Godfrey owned it in 1749. The latter or his son disposed of the aforesaid tract in smaller parcels and all of the western part is included in the ancient hamlet of Cockletown.

On the north side of the Old road there was a stone and log dwelling about where Dr. Wharton’s house stood, but closer to the road. This may have been built by Abel Thomas, carpenter, who owned about 70 acres in the vicinity, mostly in the woods, in 1783. This house was later occupied by Widow Jane Dane after she had retired from the Springhouse Tavern.

A short distance west and on the opposite side of the road there was a blacksmith shop The site was probably immediately in front of the cottage built much later by Levering Latch, where scrap iron and a cannon ball were unearthed. The late Mrs. Benjamin Longaker, nee Lewis, has said that she remembered this building from her early girlhood when it was in a tumbledown condition. It had the appearance even then of being very ancient and was reputed haunted-lights appearing in the windows as if the ghost of the blacksmith had returned and was busied relighting the forge.

The John Reese house, later the residence of the Rev. Dr. Sagebeer, doubtless dates from the Reese ownership. This, of logs, is now weather-boarded. The low, long barn dated from 1830 and was removed about 1880.

Abel Reese in his will, January 8, 1797, bequeathed to his son John, his plantation of 63 acres, he to pay his sisters Judith and Elizabeth, Â£100. The first house on this farm, was a small one of logs close to the public road, on the extreme southwest corner of that position of land north of the Old road and close to the entrance of the wood road to the valley. It was probably built by John Thomas or earlier, in Atkinson’s time. This building was removed about 1876.

The original Drove Tavern (or taverns, since the story goes that there were two connected by an underground passage) was on the site of the later Fritz house, and was reached from the Old Lancaster road by a lane. In 1779 it was said to be kept by Thomas Search; certainly, either this or the last Drove on the Turnpike was kept by John Reese and his son Abel.

On the North side of the Old road and west of the John Reese farm, was the Burns farm, as it became known. Thomas Godfrey parceled out the Standly grant in smaller lots as before mentioned; forty acres to Thomas McKean and thirty acres to John Shaw in 1750. Shaw sold to Enoch James, James transferred the same to Christian Brannaman, usually listed as “Brandy man,” and the executors of the latter to Sebastian Rink. McKean also sold to Rink.

McKean was landlord at the Blue Ball Tavern and was taxed in Easttown for 400 acres of land. He was the largest landowner there in 1765. Heretofore we have had Welsh, Scotch-Irish and English owners, but Brannaman and Rink were Germans. A marker was erected by the D.A.R. over the grave at St. Peter’s of Ensign George King, who is said to have been a younger son of a German baron. He married in 1756, Catherine, daughter of Christian Brannaman.

Rink was a shoemaker. The records show that he did not come in absolute possession of the eastern tract of 30 acres until 1765 and the western tract of 40 acres until 1769, though he was probably in residence earlier. His first assessment was erroneously from Easttown. His residence on the western tract not far from the only available spring would seem to indicate an agreement for its purchase, and it was he who replaced the original log cabin with a mansion (in those days) of thick stone gable walls and dressed log front and rear, and caused to be traced deeply in the wet mortar of a countersunk square high up in the west gable “B.R. 1767”.

In 1775, after the sale to Christopher Rue, Rink disappeared. This was not an uncommon subterfuge, during the Revolution to prevent confiscation should the Crown prevail. Rue, who was a lieutenant of the Easttown militia, conveyed the property to Andrew Steel of the Leopard Tavern, in 1779, two years after Steel, a non-combatant had conveyed it to Joseph Griffith, an officer in the Tredyffrin militia. Both officers filed lists of damages inflicted by the British army, aggregating 67 pounds, 2 shillings and 3 pence. The house was later the residence of George P. Orr, who greatly enlarged and remodeled it.

The next habitation was immediately in front of the Robert Doyle residence, long known as Peggy’s Corner, an ancient log cote which Dr. Quimby immortalized in his novel “Valley Forge” as “Peggy Hambleton’s Cake and Beer Shop.” Old English coins have been excavated here. Later the site was only a heap of stones at the foot of an ancient cedar. It was replaced by the present small house on the southeast corner of Howellville and State roads in 1846.

The last house on the Old road in Cockletown was near the former MacNamee house later occupied by S. Paul Teamer. It was a long, low structure of logs and of two periods: the easternmost section very old; the western end built later where a tenant at one time kept a night school. It was called “Corner Lott” in the 1792 will of old Abel Reese when bequeathed to wife Violetta. This tract was mainly west of the old Welsh line which ran from the Newtown Street road through Easttown. A very early owner was Richard Iddings whose daughter Elizabeth was the mother of General Anthony Wayne.

Not all of the houses of Cockletown lay close to the Old road; several were hidden in the folds of the wooded ravines leading down to the valley. In “Lewis’ Hollow”, then reached by a wood road through the Reese land, there was a tract of ten acres. The original log house was embedded in the southern slope of the hill near the upper spring.

“Neilley’s Hollow” also contained inhabitants. There was a small log cabin on the crest of the hill above the springs (in the midst of Doyle’s North Berwyn nursery). This probably belonged to the Reese family at one time. Tradition states its early tenants operated a small distille1y at the source of Trout Run immediately below, probably the Black Swan.

Of the two or three original Cockletown houses now standing, the Neilley house is the oldest. The homestead of one or more acres is said to have been part of an original grant of 100 acres to Thomas and Cadwalader Jones by right of their mother. James Neilley, according to family history, was born in 1750 in the County Antrim, Ireland, came to America in 1768, and set up a handloom for linen weaving in 1775.

This house was built of stone on the living rock, the rear buried in the side of the hill; the superstructure of logs and the original bowed roof was thatched with rye straw. It had one room in the basement, two on the first floor and an unceiled garret. The shop for weaving was an abandoned stable one and a half stories high, with earthen floor and no provision for heating. It stood immediately in front of the house and was demolished about 1880, and a small one-story annex added to the west side of the cottage, which served for a carpet weaving loom for the last Neilley, also a James. In the renovation of this old house, William Doyle was careful to retain all the outward features, so that while the interior was made comfortable, the exterior presents much of the characteristics of by gone days.

Thus did Cockletown, without plan or forethought, come into existence. It was just a typical community of its time, composed mainly of mechanics and small farmers combined, but an essential part of the rural economy of a growing colony.

Doubtless its inhabitants had front row seats for the series of important military events which took place in the neighborhood beginning in the early autumn of 1777. But with the completion of the Turnpike in 1798, Cockletown became just another backwoods settlement and passed into harmless disuse long before the Reeses erected their sign “Reeseville” opposite the Drove Tavern.
