children.text:
Chapter 5: Turnpike Period

1798 - 1833

All but the eastern end of Cockletown, on the Old Lancaster road, was in Tredyffrin, but upon completion of the Philadelphia and Lancaster turnpike in 1798 by a company of progressive business men, nearly all of the transient traffic moved to a parallel line south of old Cockletown and mostly in Easttown. 

This was the first toll road constructed in the country. The more direct route with graded and stone-paved roadbed, at once justified the expenditure by the increased stream of travelers requiring “entertainment for man and beast,” hence the numerous taverns that appeared along the road. There were drove, wagon, and stage stands, the latter being by far the best conducted.

All of the pre-Revolutionary stands left stranded on the back road were speedily put out of existence and their owners compelled to rebuild on the pike in order to hold their custom, but wherever the turnpike happened to occupy the old roadbed, the fortunate landlord opposite reaped an increased trade. Of the more fortunate were the Black Bear and the General Paoli. 

The General Paoli, named in honor of Pasquale Paoli the Corsican patriot, came to be the Democratic headquarters, the polling place of Easttown and several other townships, and by the addition of several wings, offered an imposing front. It was owned by the Evans family for over a hundred years; Joshua Evans 1769-1814, Joshua Evans jr. 1814-1846, and John D. Evans 1846 until 1873. The Evanses, however, did not keep tavern continuously, for there were several early landlords, including Richard Robinson in 1799 and for some years after. 

Joshua Evans jr. was the political and military leader of the district. Paoli was crowded on election day, the voters sometimes lined up for a quarter of a mile, and as every district had its bully, fights were numerous and often became general. The landlord on important election days disposed of two or three barrels of whiskey, besides quantities of cider, cherry bounce, and other liquors. In 1812 a regiment was mustered at the Paoli and neighboring taverns.

Isaac Wayne was also a political leader. He frequently got in difficulty at the Paoli inn when it was filled with an election or military muster crowd, and his trusted son-in-law, William Hayman, usually came to his rescue. “Isaac Wayne! Are you in trouble again?” “Yes Billy, come here!” and Billy would plunge through the packed mass, pushing men to the right and left, until he reached the side of Isaac and took his part in the fracas.

The Springhouse, the successor of the Fox tavern on the Old road, was located in what is today the east end of Berwyn It was built by William Torbert for John Llewellyn, a brother of David Llewellyn of the Fox, and in 1814 bought by the Kuglers. From 1825-1830 it was leased by John Dane, later by his widow, when it became known as “Peggy Dane’s” tavern, the rendezvous of many a rustic beau, for the landlady had a bevy of dark-eyed daughters. Later it was occupied by the owner as a residence, a member of the family that made Kugler’s restaurant famous in Philadelphia.

This tavern was situated at the head of the Darby creek, with ample yard room and an abundance of spring water. It became known as the Big tavern. Samuel White who had sold his Valley Forge farm, moved there in 1855, but after he had occupied the building a single day it caught fire from locomotive sparks and burned down. It was rebuilt on part of the old walls by the Rev. John McLeod.

The new Drove bore an evil reputation for drunken brawls and gambling. It catered to a rough class, the drovers. It was popularly believed that unknown patrons were robbed and perhaps murdered in their beds, through a system of easy entry to the bedrooms by means of trap doors from cellar to garret in superimposed closets. Here, also, scandal whispers, a sporting member of the Reese family staked a farm on the throw of the dice and lost!

The older building was demolished by Henry Fritz in 1869 to make room for his residence. Curious neighbors wished to dig in the old cellar for traces of bodies but the owner filled it up with the remark that as he expected to live there, the less he knew of former trouble the better. 

,	The Reeses appear to have been a kindly people, fond of sport of all kinds, and they naturally attracted the noisy, sporting class. They imported the first thoroughbred stallion for breeding purposes, in all this neighborhood, and the Old Lancaster road through Cockletown provided an excellent half mile dirt track upon which the improved type of horseflesh was exercised by their owners. The turnpike had drawn off most of the traffic, and the Sunday impromptu races down the Old road lined the fences and filled the trees with spectators, some of whom bet freely upon the result. Later, the Reeses built a track in a field west >of the Howellville road (later occupied by the nursery of W.H.Doyle) and altogether spent a great deal of time and money on race horses.

The new Drove stood on the northeast corner of the turnpike and the Howellville road, built against the bank so that the occupant could step from the second story rear door to his backyard, and the rear rooms of the ground floor were dark and damp to the extreme. The singularly graveyard repellent odor of the Judas tree, the enormous boxwood bushes, and the greenish unhealthy-looking fruit lying crushed under the large Osage orange, heightened the evil effect. 

It is certain that John Reese, a reputable farmer on the Old road, was the proprietor in the early 1830s and that the Rev. William Henry Rees occupied one of the buildings while preaching at St. David’s and St. Peter’s churches. Abel Reese may have been the last landlord.

Of the new hostelries, the Lamb (now Roughwood, a private residence), corner of the Turnpike and Line (Great or Baptist) road, Devon, was built about 1805 by George Rees who was later Sheriff of Philadelphia county, and a country store was kept there by Jonathan Jones, 1805-1812. John Lewis was first tavern landlord in 1813, followed by Jacob Clinger, 1815-1830.

The Stage Coach (later part of the lawn of George D. Woodside’s mansion, Devon) was owned by John Havard Davis, 181O; John Lewis, 1810-1812,-Alexander E. Finley, 1813-1830, perhaps later, and was followed by a German by the name of Shenaman, who was the last landlord. Finley was a Scotch-Irishman of some political influence anda “colonel” of the militia. The Stage was often called the “Militia house” since the Glassley commons where it was located was scene of many a military muster of Easttown.

The signs of both the Lamb and Stage were the work of a self-taught artistic genius, James McGuigan, of Glassley commons. All inns in that day had signboards with pictures on them. This was necessary, for many of the teamsters along the road could not read.

The old Blue Ball of Mt. Airy (now known as Daylesford), had been left out of the line of travel and a new tavern was erected close to the new pike. It was also known as the Blue Ball, though oftener called “Prissy’s” tavern after the notorious Prissy Robinson who kept it for many years and died, at the age of one hundred years and six months, after outliving three husbands. The estate, except a few acres, was in woods, and Prissy was for many years before her death under the necessity of selling ginger cakes and molasses candy to the children at nearby Mt. Airy school for the few pennies she could make. 

The Black Bear was the only tavern in this vicinity on the south side of the pike. It stood near where today’s Route 252 crosses Lancaster avenue and served wagoners and drovers.

The General Jackson built by Randall Evans, brother and bitter rival of the landlord of the Paoli, was headquarters for the Farmers’ Lodge of Freemasons, No. 183, from September 12, 1822 to about 1830 when it was constrained to forfeit its charter during the anti-Mason craze. Evans was succeeded by Evenson, who called it the Franklin, and it was later known as the Hinkson house. Much later it was the headquarters of the local branch of the Red Cross, during World War I.

It was the custom of the times to abbreviate the names to Stage, Ball, Bear, etc. There were 62 taverns or inns located along the 62 miles of the turnpike between Philadelphia and Lancaster.

The Paoli was a stage stand of excellent reputation. Many of the others were frequented principally by the wagoners and drovers who were usually content if they could find a spot on the barroom floor for their blankets, and sometimes while they lay in a drunken sleep, the crafty landlady would extract produce from their wagons to serve up for breakfast!

Robert McClenachan, late of Ireland, styled a Philadelphia merchant, married Amelia Harrison, who had inherited a large tract of Easttown land. In 1800, shortly after completion of the turnpike through a part of this property, McClenachan laid out on paper the new town of Glassley with wide streets, squares, and lots, on a tract about equidistant between the Lamb and Springhouse taverns.

Beginning on the north at Old Lancaster road running east and west there were in succession: “North”, “Turnpike,” “South,” and “Pearl” streets; beginning on the west running north and south there were “Green”. “Harrison,” “Franklin,” “Washington,” “Thompson (now Fairfield),” “Wayne,” and “McClenachan (now Valley Forge)” streets. But beautiful Glassley never became a town. It looked good on paper, but it had no industry to attract prospective residents.

McClenachan donated a piece of ground in his model town “on the side of the hill near a spring of water” for a school. At that time there was a schoolhouse in Howellville, one near Strafford, and one near the edge of Newtown, but all were too far away to accommodate the children of Easttown. With the ground having been provided, people gave either money or work as best they could, and in 1808 Glassley School House was completed and opened to children who could attend.

After selling some lots, the disgusted founder returned to England and there died. For many years this fenceless tract was known as the “Glassley commons.”

Here Major Wetherby, Captain Rowan, and Ensign Hampton proudly exhibited and exercised their gaudily clad militia, which later degenerated in ever more of a farce. Every male over 16 years of age was supposed to turn out once a month for military drill, according to the law. The military spirit was at low ebb and there were no active leaders and the men and boys tramped about at random, often armed with cornstalks, to fulfill the letter of the law.

Later they persuaded landlord Finley of the Stage to assume charge, dubbing him “Colonel” though he knew nothing of military matters. However, he was not loath to lead them to the field and exclaim, “Line up b’ys, line up with your backs to the turnpike and your faces to the gum tree and stand still until I gov’ the word halt!”

General Anthony Wayne was buried at Fort Erie where he died in 1796, and years later his son Isaac disinterred his bones and brought them home packed in the body of his sulky. On June 6, 1811, the local military companies assembled at Evans’ (Jackson) tavern, Paoli, and moved out the Lancaster road to meet the Norristown cavalry and the funeral cortege, which they conducted to Old St. David’s church.

Samuel Smiley, an old soldier under Wayne, insisted upon marching on foot in front of the hearse the whole distance. Chaplain David Jones was present and upon the solicitations of the assembled neighborhood, mounted the platform to relate once more the horrible details of that awful night when under the command of the cold-blooded Grey, the British surprised Wayne at Paoli.

Wayne’s war horse survived him many years and was often ridden by his son on the muster days of the militia. Col. Isaac Wayne inherited from his distinguished father a taste for military matters which he often exercised on the old Valley Forge parade grounds.

In the second war with Great Britain, or War of 1812 as it was called, local men took a prominent part. Cromwell Pearce, was appointed Major General of the Third Division, Pennsylvania Militia. Isaac Wayne was offered a colonelcy in the infantry, but refused, preferring to enlist troop. Benjamin Wetherby was Captain of the Fourth company in the 65th Regiment, Pennsylvania Militia. The local companies did not see a great deal of action, but the officers in higher command were in several hot engage-ments. In 1812 Cromwell Pearce resigned his empty title of Major General of Militia to become Colonel of the 16th U.S. Regulars, and while second in command under General Pike, captured York (now Toronto), Canada. In the battle of Chrystler’s Field near Williamsburg, Canada, November 11, 1813, in which the Americans were victorious, the command devolved to him after General Covington was mortally wounded.

It was announced during 1816 that Wetherby’s company would be paid off at the Paoli tavern on a certain date. Doubtless Joshua Evans had extra heavy receipts on the appointed day when “the ghost walked.”

On September 20, 1817, the Republican Artillerists, headed by Col. Cromwell Pearce, and with the local military companies, dedicated the first monument to the dead at Paoli. Five years later, Col. Pearce and his wife conveyed about 23 acres adjacent to the graves as a place of parade forever. The Paoli Battle had taken place next to the Pearce family farm when the Colonel was five years old.

The intrusion of government into the lives of Easttown residents was very slight. County officials (commis-sioners, judges, etc.) were situated in West Chester. Justices of the peace represented the county judges locally, but most served districts comprising three or four townships Easttown was paired with Willistown and East Whiteland. The first Easttown appointee as Justice of the Peace was Whitehead Wetherby in 1800, followed by Benjamin Wetherby in 1817.

The Fiftieth Anniversary of the evacuation of the Continental army at Valley Forge was celebrated on July 26, 1828. That late date was to accommodate the farmers who were busy with cultivation on June 20th, and harvesting crops on July 4th. It was ostensibly a Harvest Home but actually a Whig political gathering of the local admirers of the grand old sage, John Quincy Adams.

We are told that the morning was ushered in by a salute of cannon and that some venerable survivors of the Revolution were seated upon the stand with the orator of the day, Col. JC. Watmough. Abisha T. Woodman contracted to provide lunch for the entire company on thirteen tables, each 164 feet long, and seating 1600; about 3000 were fed here and many others dined elsewhere.

Jonathan Roberts presided over the dinner at which thirteen toasts were scheduled: George Washington, John Quincy Adams, Henry Clay, Richard Rush and Anthony Wayne were extrolled, and Andrew Jackson, Timothy Pickering, Livingston of Louisiana, Eaton of Tennessee, Giles of Virginia and other Democrats, condemned.

Except for commerce transacted at the taverns and inns along the pike, nearly all of Easttown’s 600 inhabitants were involved in day to day subsistence agriculture for their livelihood. Some small amount of grain crops and meat produced were considered surplus and sold at market, but the greatest portion of what the farm produced was used on the farm itself.

Most farms were fifty or more acres in size and generally stood at a distance from each other. A traveler, some years earlier, with perhaps some exaggeration, noted that between Philadelphia and Lancaster he found “not any two buildings standing together except at Downingtown.”

Opposite the fifteenth mile stone on the turnpike (Classley) Samuel Stirk, wheelwright, and Patrick McCuigan, blacksmith, were established. Blacksmiths, and often wheelwrights, flourished also near the inns at the Paoli, Leopard, and elsewhere.

The little community that served Easttown was of scarcely any importance, known at this time as the “Sixteenth mile stone,” advertised as late as 1832 by Van Leer and Channel, who had moved their stand from Tredyffrin to the “spacious store house on the Lancaster pike’ at Newtown road where they sold dry goods, groceries, and liquors; or as “Peggy Dane’s” or the “Drove.”

The coming of the railroad was soon to displace pike traffic. The road, not an engineering wonder, was as crooked as a meadow brook and was at first operated by horse power, but on April 1, 1834 the first locomotive, the “Black Hawk,” ran in eight and one-half hours from Philadelphia to Lancaster. By 1836 steam had displaced horse power. Abel Reese viewed the first steam-drawn cars with tears running down his face, and he exclaimed to his neighbor, Peter Burns sr., “Our farms are ruined!” Burns sacrificed a valuable colt racing the returning engine into Philadelphia.

The stage and freighting business on the turnpike was indeed soon ruined, and although the decline of the tavern was gradual it was more or less complete, and it was high time for the common tap-room was demoralizing the people. The barroom had become the social life of a certain proportion of the male inhabitants and swearing, quarreling, habitual drunkards infested every neighborhood.

Of the taverns before mentioned, the Lamb, Blue Ball, and Jackson became, for a time at least, private residences; the Stage, Springhouse, and Paoli were destroyed by fire; and the Drove and Black Bear were demolished.

Dr. John P. Lewis, local Quaker physician, had a wide practice. He and Dr. Thomas B. Evans, a cousin of Anthony Wayne, are said to be the first physicians to practice in Easttown. Lewis’ daybook of 1827 shows that he charged $1 for a single visit including medicine, though often no greater sum for two or three visits. He charged 25 cents for extracting a tooth or for bleeding. Vaccination came high at $1.50 to $2 and the reduction of fractured members, from thumb to leg, ran from 75 cents to $5.

Easttown residents continued to make their way on Sunday to the three old meeting houses, St. David’s, Valley Baptist, and Valley Presbyterian.

For nearly a score of years St. David’s Church was without a regular rector. Little had been done at Radnor to arouse the congregation from the spiritual apathy caused by the Revolution and the hierarchical split with the Church of England. Its pulpit was at last filled by the Rev. Samuel C. Brinckle 1818-1832, in whose term was inaugurated the first Sunday school with the venerable John Hunter as superintendant.

Then followed the Rev. William Henry Rees, 1833-1838, who was a native of Cockletown as was his father before him. The Rev. Rees, late of the Diocese of Maryland, had been called from the Church of St. James the Greater, Bristol, and left this vicinity for Mt. Vernon Institute, an Episcopal Church school at West Chester.

Dr. Henry Yates Carter was the first secretary of the St. David’s vestry of this time. He was born in London, 1750, and died at his home opposite the Drove tavern, 1849. He had been assistant surgeon on board Lord Nelson’s flagship at Trafalgar.

The Rev. David Jones was again the pastor of the Baptist Church in the Great Valley from 1792 to 1820 with frequent leaves of absence. In February, 1799, the Church was incorporated, and in 1805 a new stone meeting house was built. The oak logs of the original building were sold for $55 and dragged up Valley Forge road to be used as an addition to the Lamb tavern on the turnpike. The parsonage was built in 1816 and the barn in 1823. The little creek, Nantyr Ewig, which flows through the meadow, was dammed and here the converts were baptized at all seasons of the year until a pool was provided in the new chapel at Berwyn. It was popularly believed that no one had ever taken cold from baptism as practiced by this denomination.

In August, 1821, the Rev. Thomas and Elizabeth Roberts, Evan and Elizabeth Jones, Isaac and Rachel Cleaver, and John Farrier were dismissed to form a mission to the Cherokees in Tennessee, the first fruits of the Missionary Society organized in 1816.

It is noteworthy that after this little band of zealous Baptists had labored long to reduce the tribal dialect to a written form, they found that an illiterate half-breed Cherokee, Sequoyah, or George Guess, with nothing but a split shingle and a piece of charcoal, had devised in 1826 a syllabic alphabet by which he rendered the language completely expressive. The missionaries discarded their own attempts, although they had already printed a spelling book, and were pleased to adapt Sequoyah’s arrangement. A son of Evan Jones, the Rev. John B. Jones, born on the mission field, translated the Scriptures into Cherokee many years later.

The closing days of the Turnpike era marked a season of great religious activity under the Rev. Leonard Fletcher. It is said that during his pastorate 447 converts were baptized and 26 admitted by letter, and at this time and for more than a score of years later, especially under the leadership of the Kauffman family, the choir enjoyed an excellent reputation for music.

The Baptist Church in the Great Valley became the parent through missions of the following Church organizations: Lower Merion, 1808; Phoenixville, 1830; Norristown, 1832; Willistown, 1833; West Chester, 1834; Radnor, 1841. This last, it is true, was secession from the Great Valley church, when 79 communicants in sympathy with Rev. Fletcher’s antislavery views, asked for and received their letters to form a church in Radnor.

Great Valley Presbyterian Church had but one pastor during all of this period, the Rev. William Latta, 1799-1847. He was born in 1768 and died in 1847. He made a memorable prayer at the West Chester reception for General Lafayette in July, 1825. He was a son of the Rev. Dr. James Latta and a brother of the Rev. Francis A. Latta.

title: Chapter 6: Beginning of the Local Industrial and Educational Period
newspaper: Easttown, Old in History, Young in Spirit, 1704 - 2004 by C. Herbert Fry

children.text:
Chapter 6: Beginning of the Local Industrial and Educational Period

1834 - 1859

The	Philadelphia and Columbia railroad, an undertaking of the state “Main Line of Public Works,” was crooked, uneven, and full of high grades. Its light rails were laid in slotted iron chairs which in turn were bolted to stone sills about 22 x 14 x 12 inches or less. This proved unsatisfactory and eventually gave way to wood ties. The first cars were horse drawn and, as horseflesh is ever unequal in speed, a schedule could not be maintained. 

The first light engines had comparatively high smoke-stacks which were hinged to lower while going under the low overhead bridges, and a man had to go along the track after every train to drive in wedges loosened by vibration of the engine.

When a locomotive ran off of the track, the train crew and perhaps some of the passengers would pry it on again with a couple of fence rails. The first passenger injured met with an accident which occurred through carelessness. The man stood up in his seat to pick an apple hanging froma tree over the right of way and struck his head against a limb; he fell under the car and had a leg severed. For a long time the engines burned wood, which gave the sawyers much employment. Hugh J. Steen had a contract to furnish wood by the cord, and he often joked about certain crooked logs rejected by the sawyers which formed the base for new stacks and were measured again and again!

The Columbia railroad was commenced previous to 1828 and completed in 1833. The first train hauled by the famous ’Black Hawk” locomotive passed over the road on the last day of February, 1834. The Pennsylvania Railroad, incorporated April 13, 1846, built a road from Harrisburg to Pittsburgh and took over the old Columbia road on August 1, 1857. The railroad was originally surveyed in 1826, on a line in the Great Valley near the northern slope of the South Valley hills from Warren tavern to the gap opposite Spread Eagle, where it was planned to enter the hills. This would leave Paoli inn, which had so long been enriched by social, political, and military preferment, high and dry. Joshua Evans jr. was a man of energy and of influence, however, and he pulled every wire to have the railroad pass his door.

The story is told that a gang employed in some preliminary work was quartered at the Davis tavern, Howellville, which was on the proposed railroad. Something had gone wrong at the hotel; the landlord was inclined to be grouchy, and the men complained that they were not getting good service. The hostler, doubtless an emissary of Evans, intimated that if they would go to the Paoli inn they would be treated right. It appears that they went to Paoli and were kept dead drunk for five days during which time the officials were vainly searching for them and wild rumors spread of their capture by Indians.

It is possible that the valley was the ostensible route projected to obtain concessions from the owners along the turnpike, but at any rate Joshua Evans felt that he had obtained a victory, as indeed he had. The Paoli inn was admirably situated to cater to the increased trade that the trains brought to its doors. The bustle of the military muster and elections was succeeded by the rush of passengers to eat and “liquor up,” but after some years of prosperity the roadbed and equipment improved so much that the time to and from Philadelphia became all too brief to admit of lengthy stops; from this time on the Paoli inn gradually declined.

To the east, the community dwelling near the “Sixteenth Mile Stone” on the turnpike settled down to a long period of quiet, simple, rural life. A few buildings had sprung up between the Springhouse and Drove taverns, notably John Lewis’ (later Frank Matson’s) log house, William Sloanaker’s store on the corner of Newtown (later Waterloo) avenue. William Gamble's single and double stone houses, better known as the cigar factory because of the Spanish and half-Spanish cigars made there, and a few other buildings including a store-house for grain from the valley on the northwest corner of Howellville road and Lancaster pike across from the Drove Jonathan Moore’s, formerly Dampman’s, a drover). The farmhouses of the Carters, Potters, Wetherbys and Smiths were close by. It formed a somewhat modernized duplicate of the ancient hamlet of Cockletown.

A small frame and plaster office had been erected early in the century for the use of Dr. John Wilson Rees until his death in 1840 in the 34th year of his age. This stood opposite the Drove, between the pike and railroad. Here the Rev. William Henry Rees, rector of Old St. David’s and St. Peter’s, established a Sunday school with 45 scholars and three teachers in 1837, and here Clara Davis kept a private school in 1865.

The indefatigable Rev. Rees also established a select school for boys in his residence at the Drove tavern until his removal to West Chester in 1839, to devote his whole time to his Mount Vernon Academy.

This easternmost building, sometimes called the Drove, was then occupied until 1850 by Noble Heath and his Reeseville Boarding school. In this connection it is well to mention that Noble Heath, in 1855, published “A Treatise on Arithmetic,” which was very superior and very complete. 

The place was not of sufficient importance to justify even a flag stop on the railroad; the turnpike had become almost deserted and badly out of repair, yet it became apparent that the village needed a name. About 1835 a sign appeared on the little schoolhouse announcing “Reeseville” to all who passed. The Reese family was among the early Welsh settlers of the neighborhood and the name was the logical one for the place, though it created considerable criticism and some opposition.

The Sloanaker store had recently been leased by a man named Clarence, and after he renovated the buildings he put up a sign “Clarenceville”. Not to be outdone, Rev. Rees put up a board in his meadow opposite Clarence’s store, lettered “Mount Vernon,” apparently were never generally accepted, and the village settled into a comfortable familiarity with the name Reeseville for the next forty years.

Before the establishment of the public school system a few scholars attended private academies, but so called “pay” or subscription schools were the norm. Youths in Easttown usually attended at the Wayne school, on the border of Wayne’s plantation, along Bear road and a few hundred feet north of the Bear tavern, or at the Glassley school south of the Lancaster turnpike, in McClenachan’s Classley development, where “reading, writing, spelling, and ciphering” were taught. In common with the parochial school at St. David’s church, they were all tiny, one-room affairs capable of accommodating an average, perhaps, of fifteen or twenty children. The masters often taught school in the winter when farm work was light and worked as a farm hand in the summer.

With the implementation of the Common School Act, in 1835 and later, the trustees managing each school were replaced by an elected board of township school directors. School tuition was eliminated in favor of tax support which came partly in the fonn of levied school taxes and partly in the fonn of a subsidy from the state. The St. David’s school was torn down by the church in 1844, but two new schools were added by Easttown township.

Foundations were dug for a school on Church road between the Smith and the Adam Siter farms. Adam Siter was the schoolmaster of the Old Eagle school - “Hop and Go Fetchit” the boys called him. However this site was not used, for John Ogden of Hickory Hill about 1850 offered a part of his ground and $500 to build on the site selected by him; this became known as the Ogden school which name it retained even after the old building and site were abandoned for the new one just below.

The Leopard school was built about 1852, on Leopard road behind the old inn. It was originally one story but a second was added in 1872 being designed for a town hall for elections, school entertainments, political meetings, the lyceum, religious services, etc. It replaced the Wayne school and became the most efficient school in Easttown.

The Public School Report for 1865 shows that Easttown had three schools, Glassley, Ogden, and Leopard; a nine-months term, 76 male and 82 female scholars; the male eacher receiving $35 and the female teacher $30 a month. The school and building tax was 4.5 mills, a total tax for the year of $1694. Tredyffrin seemed less forward to school provision though in the aggregate spent a larger sum. There were nine schools Howellville, Presbyterian, Tablet (Salem), Walker's (near Calder’s blacksmith shop), New Centerville (Fairfield), Carr’s, Eagle and Mt. Airy, with a seven-months term, 177 male and 145 female scholars; paying teachers $28 alike; the tax was 6.25 mills and amounted to the sum of $2554 for the year.

The Tredyffrin side of Reeseville attended the Mount Airy school along the turnpike on bleak Skelp Level (now Daylesford), sharing the single room of the stone building with the youths and maidens of Paoli. This school was adjacent to Prissy Robinson’s of Blue Ball notoriety, and now and then Prissy stormed the school door, ax in hand, in pursuit of some offending pupil.

She had a perpetual grudge against the railroad for destroying the tavern business. One day a locomotive killed her heifer which had wandered upon the track. Prissy rendered the tallow and greased the track. A late train tried all night to reach Paoli, and the ancient crone stood on her doorstep, shook her fist and swore she would give them tallow as long as the dead heifer held out! The next day an official came from Paoli and settled for the cow.

The decade of the 1840s appeared to be the time of reconstruction and replacement of many of the old log buildings with the more durable stone. Masons were in demand more or less steadily every season up to about 1851, at a daily wage of from $1.00 to $1.47 and ½ for masons and 50 cents a day for tenders.

During harvest time the weaver, mason, carpenter, and able-bodied men of various other trades quitted their normal occupations to help the farmer gather his crops. This condition of affairs was extremely advantageous to the farmer, for it gave him help close at hand just when he needed it, and at the same time it was beneficial to the artisan in the matter of cash and change of labor. Old timers enthused upon the sight of ten or a dozen expert reapers, cradles in hand, encircling a field of golden grain. The day began at 6 a.m. and ended at 7 p.m., with an hour for noon and short rests at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m. for lunch. Five meals a day found!

A farmer on what was later the Sharp farm paid in cash every evening after supper the day’s wage of sixty-two and a half cents. One afternoon at 5:30 o'clock a thunderstorm drove the harvesters to the house for an early supper, and their employer passed from one to another with the “cash upon the nail” reiterating, “Three-quarters and half a quarter” until he reached the last, who happened to be an Irishman, who refused to be docked an eighth of a day, exclaiming, “A whole day or nothing!” The mildly astonished farmer paid him in full, and, after another visit to his strong box, painstakingly refunded to every man in pennies and half pennies the amount for “half a quarter” day.

Squire Benjamin Wetherby, an old bachelor who owned much land south of Reeseville, was something of a character. Tradition states that he once collected a debt through the devious processes of law from Prissy Robinson and that she paid it with a barrel of large copper pennies and half pennies, remarking that, “The counting will give the old devil something to do!” 

Wetherby took great delight in the parade of the militia, in fact he once commanded the 38th Regiment. One evening, sometime in the 1830s, a small barefoot boy on a nearby farm heard the sound of fifes and drums issuing from the front of the cigar factory where a newly married couple had settled. He ran as far as the railroad bridge and there halted, for it held the proud figure of Squire Wetherby who, with cane at shoulder, paraded back and forth all by himself, and the boy heard him exclaim in a voice pitched high with emotion, “Benjamin Wetherby! Justice of Peace! Major of Militia! My! How I love martial music!”

It must not be supposed that military science and leadership of this neighborhood had wholly degenerated into showy parade, a volley of blank cartridges and a rally around the bar of the tavern, for this section continued to produce leaders of the game of war. Israel Vodges of Paoli was admitted to West Point July 1, 1830, and commissioned 2nd Lieutenant, 1st Regular Artillery, July 1, 1837, and Samuel B. Hayman accredited to the same place was admitted July 1, 1838, and commissioned in the 1st Regular Infantry, July 1, 1842. Both these officers attained the grade of Brigadier General for meritorious conduct on the field of battle.

In the early days Easttown and Tredyffrin were more evenly divided between the Whig and Democrat, and elections were bitterly contested. The astute county politicians used to wait eagerly for these township returns, especially on account of the old saw, “As Easttown goes, so goes the county.” In 1840 the Easttown polls were removed from Paoli to the sign of the Leopard, kept by Philip Kirk, the political if not the geographical center of the township; and in 1843 Tredyffrin removed to the Ramrod, kept by Evans Kendall, at New Centerville.

Valley Forge continued to be a great rallying place for the Whigs. In 1840 many thousand persons were present at a Harrison meeting to hear the great Daniel Webster speak. Four years later the protective tariff was an issue and there was a long procession in which various industries were represented, including nails and other articles being manufactured, in the moving column. A rival company of Democrats followers of Polk were rushed by the Clay adherents, and the Polk stalks of their political enemies were strewn along the route.

In 1852, during the Scott-Pierce presidential campaign an ox roast was given to the many thousand people present in one of the clay pits. Protection of home industries resulted in the development of water power for the early Scotch-Irish handlooms, and the English immigrants, deprived at a livelihood at home, found it profitable with limited capital, to run small independent mills on tiny but never-failing streams in more or less remote localities. Nearly all of the local textile mills were just beyond the bounds of our township, but nevertheless added to the wealth and industry of our inhabitants. William Crosley bought 178 acres of land on Darby creek below the Easttown line and in 1828 erected a woolen mill and conducted a large business for many years until the factory burnt down. It passed into the possession of Dr. Henry Pleasants in 1861 and from him in 1865 to Casper S. Garrett, who erected a paper mill. Unfortunately, some years later this mil too was destroyed by fire.

At Valley Forge, Brooke Evans of Sheffield, England, leased the property, converting the saw and rolling mills vacated by James Wood into a gun factory, and made 20,000 rifles of a beautiful pattern. The mill was later enlarged and converted into a cotton and woolen factory which prospered a long time.

The only woolen factory in Tredyffrin was located in Howellville on the swift little stream that comes down from Prissy’s hollow, known as Crabby Creek today. The original mill was leased from about 1835 to 1850 by Robert Webster and his two sons, John and Joseph. They were from Yorkshire, England and expert in the manufacture of woolen cloth, blankets, etc. The dam was an eighth of a mile above the village, the breast now part of a farmhouse lane, and the race is still traceable down the meadow.

There was a time , about 1845, when five or six men were employrf in carding, spinning, and weaving flax in the old store shop on Howellville road on the property later known as Doyle”s Nursery.

The old Hammer Hollow tiltmill owned by J. B. Newman was converted intoa bobbin factory by William Cundy, an Englishman, and in some of the small teant houses below the high dam breast of this remote hive of industry, a cigar factory was managed by the elderly Brown who employed several workmen. The cheap Spanish and half-Spanish cigars were rolled on the benches and tied up in bunches of a hundred each without boxes. Brown later became afflicted with a religious mania, climbed up on the great water wheel, jumped off, and killed himself one night.

The spools or bobbins were slender and perfect little articles made of dogwood, which Mrs. Cundy placed in bags, heaped into a cart drawn by “Fatty”, her horse, to the Eagle station, where they were shipped to various destinations. The bobbin factory stood just below the high dam buttressed by outstanding cliffs capable of withstanding enormous pressure. The remains of the lower dam, similarly positioned, can still be located, but the turning mill of pre-Revolutionary times, and the stone cottages have disappeared entirely.

The decline of the small operator began with the perfection of steam power, great improvements in machinery, and the introduction of large capital, which permitted the scrapping of equipment about once in every seven years to keep up with American labor-saving devices. Then, too, the English-born owners made so much money at the start that they fell into expensive habits. Gradually the little country factories, so far removed from the market and lacking cheap and quick transportation, became abandoned and soon fell into ruins.

Although Reeseville eventually became the generally accepted name of the place, it had not gained local popularity as late at 1847 when Lodge No. 290 of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows was instituted, for it was officially known as Paoli Lodge. It met in the little stone building at the head of the lane of the Old Drove (later the residence of H.B. Rumrill), on the Old Lancaster road opposite the Burns homestead. Two years later the institution of an encampment composed only of Scarlet Degree members was known as the Paoli Encampment, No. 89, in the new Odd Fellows hall built in 1848 at Howellville by Hugh J.Steen, who had a store on the first floor.

The Paoli Lodge became very prosperous with several hundred members drawn from a wide extent of territory. Mr. Ritner, father of Rev. Ritner, then living in the little log house about where Dr. Okie’s gate posts later stood on the Old road, served oyster stews below stairs, especially to members driving long distances. After a time some members succeeded in having the lodge removed to Holly Martin’ s in Paoli, opposite the Bear tavern on the turnpike, and the large membership eventually split up into half a dozen lodges situated at Radnor, Newtown Square, Sugartown, Pickering, Valley Forge and Port Kennedy.

The parent lodge later returned to Howellville and met over Beitler’s store, and after some years it again removed to Paoli on Darby road where it erected the present hall.

“Paoli Grove” for a time was a popular Sunday resort about 1850. The railroad put in a switch at the Bear and ran excursions from Philadelphia until it became the resort of toughs and an unbearable nuisance to the neighborhood, when it was discontinued.

The road leading from the old Fox tavern to Wilson’s corner was opened about 1854 after a great deal of contention among the small landowners over the almost impossible grade, and the name, Contention lane, appears on later deeds.

Abel Lewis and his son Jonathan owned the small place by a spring below the Old road and between the Valley Baptist road and Contention lane. It was subsequently sold to their cousin Jackson. Jonathan kept a carpenter and coffin shop and was the father of Eugene Lewis and Mary McClure. George Lewis, uncle of Abel, resided near the head of another spring a few hundred yards west across Contention lane and was the father of Morris and Washington Lewis.

Joseph Lewis, father of Lewis Lewis, plasterer, lived on the Old road. Westley Jones bought the double house, used as a cabinet-makers shop and dwelling, and carried on shoe-making until he sold to a family of Whites, one of whom married his son Robert many years later.

Bill Laws, a colored man, lived in the old log house on the hill back of Neeley’s after it was vacated by Philip Upright and worked at “tending” mason for Isaac Burns as early as 1848.

Mordecai Davis, son of Joseph Davis of Willistown, lived on a farm at Waterloo Mills from about 1800. The property belonged to his wife, who owned it with her sister. Mordecai bought the sister’s share. He and his wife are buried at Radnor Meetinghouse. The land passed to son, John W Davis, who continued to farm and enlarge the property. In 1850, through a sheriff’s sale, he purchased the parcel across the road containing the mill. For a short time the Davis family controlled the entire community of Waterloo Mills, including the only gristmill in Easttown township.

Through the influence of John W. Davis, it is said, Waterloo Mills on January 1, 1853 became the first post office in Easttown. Tenant miller William Steele, Davis’ brother-in-law, was postmaster. Stephen Stout, the mail carrier from the Spread Eagle, often carried the mail in his hat or pocket, and the chance patrons were apt to find the day's mail lying on a stump in the woods where the carrier was engaged in felling trees. This post office was discontinued September 25, 1867.

Old-fashioned people insisted on calling the place “Cabbagetown,” a name originating about 1830 when a greedy miller became unscrupulous in the amount of toll exacted from the grain delivered by nearby farmers; to “cabbage” in old English was to purloin or steal. The name stuck long after this miller had departed for lack of customers.

There were also half a dozen houses and a blacksmith and wheelwright shop. Charles Stout was here for fifteen years, and his son, D. Bernard Stout, established a general blacksmith and carriage business from about 1865 when he returned from the Civil War, to 1891, when the old shops were replaced by a more modern stone building. After that, he operated with the aid of his son Frank until the shop was abandoned. “Nard” Stout was a thorough mechanic of the old school, able to build and finish a carriage from wheel to top-wood and iron.

A quarter of a mile above on the road leading out to the Newtown road above “Pinchtown” on	Darby creek stood the old sawmill of	Jonathan T. Morris, son of James and Honoria (Thomas) Morris, who was born in 1805 and operated the mill “up to 1843,”	followed later by Eber Beaumont. Neal, Van	Leer, and others with stout teams hauled great	logs here to be converted into boards and timbers. The dam was a good one of several acres in extent, but finally it burst, carrying the Cabbagetown dam with it. The latter was repaired but the former was not. It is now a tussock swamp and maple thicket; the boulder-faced dam is filled with soil and the old left-sided race may still be traced to the site of the mill.

The only other saw mill in Easttown stood on the same stream at Judson Campbell’s place on the west side of Newtown road at South Leopard road, just north of the Darby creek bridge, where years ago the ruins of the old wheel and timbers could be detected midst the sycamore trees. This mill also at one time ground plaster.

A small but thriving village of about fifty inhabitants had grown up around the Leopard tavern on the Darby road a mile and a half south of Wayne’s manor house. The tavern operated for almost a hundred years and was licensed last in 1863.

The village was mapped as Evansville by John Kauffman, a rising young surveyor, about 1858, in honor of his wife’s family, owners of the tavern and some other property, but like some vaccinations it did not take. The Leopard comprised the tavern (later a store kept by John W. Hayman), blacksmith shop, Porteus’ store, and perhaps eight or ten dwellings with many more houses within a short distance, making it undoubtedly the only considerable hamlet in Easttown at this time.

William Porteus was the Justice of Peace and storekeeper (later Kelley residence), and Still’s little store on the road to Willistown contributed to its activities, though it did not become a post office, under John Hayman, until April 2, 1866. Samuel Buley carried the mail from Reeseville at a yearly recompense of $100, and he was followed by George Stanley at a $50 increase.

The Darby road became for a time the Plank road in the early 1850s but soon wore out. Squire Porteus’ son was killed by the stumbling of his horse in a hole on this road. 

“Sawmill Woods” on the Yerkes place between Leopard road to Newtown and Waterloo road to the same place, about three- quarters of a mile east of Leopard, is so called because a steam sawmill operated there for some years to supply timber for the Plank road. The planks were two inches thick and laid upon sleepers. The project was abandoned about 1857, however, when the tolls collected were not sufficient to maintain the road and replace worn or rotted timbers. The remaining planks were sold to the highest bidder.

The temperance wave that swept over the country about this time resulted in numerous lodges of the Sons of Temperance being organized and their halls erected. A "“Sonny’s” hall was built on the road to the Leopard, half a mile south of Reeseville, and undoubtedly it did some good even if some of its members would occasionally blackslide. The activities of this laudable secret order were apparently short lived, since the hall was vacant in the early 1870s and remodeled for a dwelling about 1875. Eventually it was torn down.

The winter of 1856 - 1857 was remarkable for a great snowstorm which buried the railroads for a week or more. Evans boarded the stranded passengers at the Paoli inn until the trainscould be shoveled out. This winter was long remembered for the thirteen weeks of sleighing.

R. E. Lewis kept a general store at Lewis’ corner. now known as Wyola, and his trace extended throughout Easttown. His daybook of 1856 shows the prevailing prices of the staples of the period. Flour $7.50, corn meal .75 - $1.29, and potatoes 0.28 a bu., sugar .07 - .10, coffee .16, tea $1,00, rice .10, cheese .12, butter .25, crackers .08, and soap .05 - .06 a lb., vinegar .10 - .16; and molasses .65 a gal., salt .16 a bag; eggs .12 - .16 a doz., tobacco .12 - .37 a lb.; meat shoulders and hams .10 - .14, veal .10, and pork .06 - .16a lb.; boots .88 - 3.50, shoes .45 - $1.31 apr.; hats .12 - $1., shirts .75 - .88, coats or pants $1.25, muslin, print, drill, anf gingham .10 - .13 a yd.

St. Davids Church: The Rev. Willie Peck, 1838 -1845, should not bring up visions of an effeminate youth for he is said to have been six feet four inches tall and to have fought under General Pike at Toronto and General Jackson at New Orleans. He was the first resident rector of St. Davids, for the original rectory was built during his term of office.

The Rev. Breed Batcheller, 1845 - 1847, and the Rev. John A. Childs, 1848 - 1850, had very short tenure, the latter “at a salary of $350 or more if it can be raised” explains the reason Rev. Rees devoted his latter days to school teaching. An infant child of Rev. Batcheller is buried in the churchyard. The Rev. Henry G. Brown, 1851 - 1855, and the Rev. Richardson Graham, 1851 - 1861 followed

Baptist Chruch in the Great Valley: The pastors were the Rev. Charles B. Keys, 1841 - 1845; the Rev. James F. Brown, 1846 - 1854; the Rev. George Spratt, 1854 - 1858, and the Rev. William M. Whitehead, 1856 - 1861. The Church was noted for the large number of ministerial and missionary candidates raised from membership during this period.

Many of the Baptists had long been abolitionists and some of the Radnor members are known to have maintained stations on the “underground railroad.” The Clingers reserved a room on the ground floor for runaway slaves, and many a black man sat down at their breakfast table who had not been present the evening before. Apparantly John Milton Campbell of Easttowns Willowdale farm also was interested in abolitionist activities.

At Great Valley Presbyterian Church, the Rev. William R. Brigham, a native of York County, Pennsylvania followed the long ministry of the Rev. Latta and served from 1848 to 1859. A split in the Presbyterian church occurred in 1835 between the conservative old school and the more liberal new school which was more pronounced against slavery. The two constituties reunited after the Civil War.

Chapter 7: Civil War and Reconstruction

1860 - 1875

When Reeseville was so named there were only a log house and a store between the Springhouse and the Drove. In 1860 the village was a widely scattered community of about thirty houses and no local industries beyond farming and small trades. 

There were on the Lancaster pike, beginning at Glassley, the homes of J. Root, Robert Gamble, Joseph C. Smith farm (later Wynburne), Thomas Mathews (later Francis), John Kugler, Charles Thompson (later Matson), S.D. Hunter store occupied by Milton Fussel, single and double dwellings of Robert White, J. Brooke (Fritz), Mrs. Williamson (Drove), and Mrs. Jonathan Moore, nearly all with small farms attached. Leopard road: Mrs. Carter, Mrs. W.A. Potter and Stephen M. Leamy farms,- Waterloo avenue (Newtown road): Benjamin Wetherby farm. 

On the Old Lancaster road there were the small houses of J. Gowdy, George White, T. Williamson, Peggy Dane, Abel Reese, Peter Burns farm, J. Brooke (Old Drove), and Mrs. Reese (later Bentz). Howellville road: John Neeley, Robert Neeley, and Richard Evans farm,- Contention lane: B. Suplee and George Lewis small farms, with some other small parcels of land not considered of sufficient importance to map. A family of Whites in which there were several grown daughters, lived in the little house of logs (Dr. Okie gateway) and during the Civil War made flags for the government.

The frame store and dwelling on the southeast corner of Lancaster pike and Waterloo avenue had a variety of tenants, few of whom made ends meet in a community able to supply most of its own necessities. William Sloanaker, Van Leer and Channel, Clarence, Hunter, Fussel, et al., have already been named as former merchants, and there had been another, one John Law, who married Eliza Bell, daughter of the proprietor of the little store in the old Fox tavern on the Old road. He had been a sober industrious young man when he moved into this building and stocked up with the usual line of liquors in addition to general merchandise. 

Milton Fussel, father of the well known physician of a later period, was here 1859-1861, at least, during which time the property was in the name of S.D. Hunler. Fussel was the first postmaster when Reeseville received official sanction in 1861. George W Downing succeeded him in 1867.

Isaac A. Cleaver occupied the store in 1868 and a year later was named postmaster. In 1870, Cleaver built a large frame store and dwelling a square east of the old store and of course moved the post office.

Henry Fritz of the Gulph road near Carr school, an enterprising carpenter and builder who had made a stake in the Askin’s operations at Wayne, married local girl Mary Lobb on December 24, 1863 and settled here soon after. He built himself a mansion, the coal, lumber, and feed warehouses, and the four tenant houses (west of Howellville road on the Turnpike) known as the Brown row or “Scienceville.” He was deservedly popular, took great interest in the welfare of the church and the building of the parsonage, but unfortunately his life was cut short by an accident at the Eagle railroad grade crossing in 1870.

Rev. McLeod built the blacksmith, wheelwright and saddler shops, the cottage in which Sammy Buley village sexton lived, and a triple dwelling known as the “Beehive.” Joseph Ernst farmed for the McLeods and John Mains, popular young man, was the village blacksmith.

Charles L. Thompson, president of a street car line in Philadelphia, built the double house where “Jake’s” store (Lichtenfeld’s) later stood. His family was a live one: Charles, Joseph, William, Morton, Hetty, perhaps others, and they were fond of sport and horses. A married daughter and her family, the Parks, occupied one side.

Strange though it seems, Reeseville did not appear on the schedule of the Pennsylvania railroad as late as 1871. The neighborhood was distinctly agricultural. The Lamb was occupied by the Clingers, the Stage by Eber Beaumont and the Leopard by Mrs. Evans, all as private residences. Miss Finley lived in a small house east of the Stage, which her brother kept so long. Mrs. Dane moved into what was once Cockletown on the Old road, in a house soon to be pulled down to make room for Clayton Lobb’s modern house. Her daughters were all married and living near by. 

Abel Reese puttered about his farm in summer and shot game for the market during the fall and winter. He was a crack shot with a sawed-off shot gun and received 25 cents a brace for quail or rabbits, double that sum for woodcock and pheasants.

Easttown’s sole grist mill, Waterloo Mills, was owned by J. W. Davis, and Tredyffrin’s Great Valley Mills, owned by Joseph Jeanes, operated with M. Beaver and Lewis L. Worrell, 1864, as miller; a combination grist and saw mill up the north branch of Valley creek operated by G. Pechin, and a saw, sometimes a sorgham, mill, by G. Clemens, on the south branch. The textile mills of Samuel Wood at Howellville and the bobbin factory of William Cundy at Hammer Hollow were still in operation. There were blacksmith and wheelwright shops at Paoli, Leopard, Waterloo Mills and Glassley, and general country stores at Black Bear, Reeseville and Leopard; though most of the inhabitants transacted much of their business in the larger towns.

The “home” town of lower Tredyffrin was Norristown, and Phoenixville was considered the same by part. Easttown patronized Newtown, Media, and Philadelphia, and the neighborhood of Paoli dealt in Malvern, which was becoming a thriving village commercially; West Chester was of course the resort for legal and political business. Had these townships been placed according to the inhabitants’ preference socially, economically and geographically, lower Tredyffrin would have been attached to Montgomery, and Easttown to Delaware county.

Many of the Easttown farms received names: Hawthorne, Fairview, Green Bank, Rockwood, Hillside, Evergreen, Sunnyside, Willowdale, and Sharon, an innovation not yet in vogue in Tredyffrin, and no longer bore the names of old Welsh settlers.

A more recent wave of Scotch and Scotch-Irish immigration had distributed in this neighborhood many farmers possessed of the requisite perseverance and rigid economy to thrive upon the hill soil, for after the first bloom of the virgin soil the farms had become poor and sold cheaply. The new owners were seldom really natural and skillful agriculturists, their maxim was not that of the German-American, “A rich farm makes a rich farmer,” but they made an attempt, at least, to maintain the balance of nature, taking off no more than they put in the soil, and as a class, with their alert intellects, were a distinct asset to the community.

There had been Union, followed by Presbyterian services, in Dr. Reese’ s office opposite the Drove, as early as 1849, but the incoming Scotch-Irish Presbyterians longed for a church of their own. The Rev. John McLeod, who had recently bought and set up his residence at the unoccupied Springhouse tavern farm formerly owned by the Kuglers, gave the site for the church building and laid out the intersecting streets as well. Ground was broken on September 28, 1861, and the following year the building was dedicated free of debt. On January 4, 1863, a few days after Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation freed the slaves, the congregation, known as Trinity Presbyterian Church, was officially organized with 20 founding members. Thus was the first church erected in Easttown, a township then in operation for almost one hundred and sixty years. Rev. McLeod became the first minister serving as “stated supply” until 1864.

The Civil war stirred the community as it never had been stirred before. The churches, which had almost without exception advocated anti-slavery, now reaped what they had sown for all loyal citizens were called upon to sustain the cause by vote and taxation if not by force of arms. The Republicans quite generally supported Lincoln’s war measures. The Democratic voters split; many of them soon became known as War Democrats; while a minority bitterly opposed to coersion were known as Copperheads. The primary motive to oppose all innovations is ingrained in the character of some people; with others it is, no doubt, coupled with a sense of loss of political prestige or the passing away of some long established privileges.

John D. Evans, owner of the Paoli inn, was a Southern sympathizer. It is said that he swore that he would not cut his beard until the South triumphed, and in consequence he wore his long whiskers buttoned under his waistcoat until his death. The Lincoln administration removed the Paoli post office to Green Tree, where it remained although still known as “Paoli”, until Johnson came into power. Thus the one time powerful Evans regime lost its last prop and Howellville became the political center of Tredyffrin.

Twenty-five or thirty years before the opening of the Civil war, the community had sent two of its brightest young men to be educated at West Point, and they were still in the Regular Army and with their military training, at the disposal of the government. One was Samuel B. Hayman of Easttown, who graduated at West Point and received his commission as Second Lieutenant of the 1st Infantry, July I, 1842; Captain March 3, 1855; Colonel New York Volunteers September 22, 1861; Brevet Lieutenant Colonel regular service, May 3, 1863, for gallant and meritorious services in the battle of Chancellorsville; mustered out of volunteer service, June 22, 1863; Brevet Colonel May 6, 1864, for gallant and meritorious services in the battle of the Wilderness; Brevet Brigadier General of Volunteers, March 13, 1865, for gallant and meritorious services in the battle of Fair Oaks, Virginia; Lieutenant Colonel 17th Infantry September 15, 1867. He retired July 1, 1872 and died May 1, 1895 in Missouri.

At the beginning of the war there was plenty of raw material. The second floors of the Leopard and Howellville schoolhouses were requisitioned for armories to accom-modate the “Home Guards.” Apparently no effort has ever been made locally to record the names of our enlisted men, a most difficult proposition at this late date, since the boys most eager to go joined singly and in small groups various regiments as opportunity permitted, and drafted men were assigned different organizations also. In fact, there was not a single company composed entirely of Easttown or Tredyffrin recruits. Natives of these two townships joined at West Chester, Phoenixville, Norristown, Philadelphia, Chester and even Harrisburg, the regiments of their choice.

A resident of Howellville, John Eyre Webster, had the honor to be one of the First Defenders. Leaving a wife and six young children in the care of his father-in-law at Reeseville, he joined the Allentown Greys mustered in the U.S. service April 18, 1861; he later served as quartermaster sergeant and died at Baton Rouge, Louisiana, June 21, 1864, from fever contracted in the Red River expedition.

Doubtless more local volunteers appear on the muster rolls of the 97th Infantry, commanded by Col. Henry R. Guss of West Chester, than of any other. The Rev. WM. Whitehead of the Baptist Church in the Great Valley was its first Chaplain. Three members of his church, Henry Kauffman jr., Isaac A. Cleaver and James J. Dewees, enlisted in Company C, which was known as the Paoli Guards, because the first recruits were raised at Leopard near Paoli. The Baptist boys tented together until the first was promoted to a lieutenancy; the second, wounded in the heel at Cold Harbor, became a sergeant; and the last as corporal on one occasion commanded the Company while going into action, received a scalp wound from a spent ball, and later was invalided home after receiving a flesh wound through both knees while advancing on the skirmish line. Each member of this trio subsequently became deacons in the Baptist Church.

Company K, the Wayne Guards, was commanded by Captain William Wayne, who later became Major of the 82nd Volunteers, but soon left the service on account of his health. Company F, in which Lewis P. Malin went out as Lieutenant and later was promoted to Captain, contained some local men.

John, brother of Henry Kauffman, enlisted as a musician, and Henry, a brother of James Dewees, was in the three months service. Joseph Dewees was so enraged at his boys for enlisting that he exclaimed: “I hope the Rebels gobble up all of you!” The hired man said, “Why Joe, if the Rebels gobble them up, they will come on and take all you got, cattle, grain and all!” “I would drive the cattle into some thicket and hide them,” answered he in some doubt. “But they would find them and give you nothing.”

Henry C. Burns, farmer, of Reeseville, was rejected at West Chester recruiting office on account of his teeth. He went to Harrisburg and there enlisted in Company H, 7th Pennsylvania Cavalry (Wynkoop’s Troop) which was transferred at once to the Army of the West. Early in 1864 he returned home on a furlough and conducted some new recruits to the camp when the regiment was recruited up to 1800 strong for the final drive. Burns was struck with a musket ball in the leg at the battle of Gaylesville, Alabama on October 21. He died in the hospital at Chattanooga on November 19, 1864 and is buried in the National Cemetery near there.

Preston Lobb enlisted on August 9, 1861, in Battery F, 5th United States Artillery (Ayres’ Battery). The artillery held attraction for a recruit; generally artillerymen got to ride in wagons, avoiding long marches that infantrymen made, and they were not assigned to dangerous picket duty. Nonetheless, Lobb saw action in some of the fiercest fighting of the war, at Ball’s Bluff, the Peninsula campaign, Antietam, and Gettysburg. At the end of his three-year enlistment in the summer of 1864, he came home (the Lobb family owned a large farm located along both sides of Sugartown road south of Reeseville), one of only five men in Battery F who was not a war casualty; the unit had numbered 295 men.

Ethelbert and Clayton Lobb, two of Preston’s brothers, entered the service in 1864 before he arrived home. Ethelbert was a recruit who returned to camp with Henry Burns to serve with Company H, 7th Pennsylvania Cavalry, during the last year of the war. Clayton served with Company N, 192nd Pennsylvania Infantry, one of the “100 day” units called up in July when Confederate General Jubal Early again threatened invasion of Pennsylvania.

Samuel H. Tompkins, born in the original log house in Lewis’ hollow, enlisted in Birney’s “Fire Zouaves” of Philadelphia. He had been associated with Good Will Fire Company and grown tough Before their departure they had marched to the church, heard a sermon on patri-otism and received pocket testaments. Early in Sam’s army life, on one occasion he drank heavily and broke all restraint. He said that when the Captain ordered him gagged with a frosty bayonet, balled and chained, and placed standing on the head of a barrel, he beat in the head, fell through and rolled down the hill. The Colonel came up and reprimanded the Captain with the remark, “I know they are bad, but I will not have their mouths ruined so they are not fit to fight. If I hear of you doing this again I will have you served the same way!” With the aid of a comrade, he learned to write while in the army and came out an industrious and trustworthy man.

When Lee’s Army of Virginia crossed over the border of Pennsylvania to Gettysburg, it was thought that they outstripped and outgeneraled the Army of the Potomac and that nothing would stop them from marching down the Lancaster pike to Philadelphia. Robert Glenn, farmer and drover on the old Blue Ball farm at Mt. Airy and reputed Copperhead, became alarmed and rode out to the neighboring farms of JW Sharp and William Wayne, with the oft repeated query, “What are you going to do? They will slaughter all our cattle!” Wayne replied that he was going to send his family to Philadelphia and himself remain on the farm.

As Early’s scouts appeared above Wrightsville on the western banks of the Susquehanna, the Union troops, including the City troop, retreated across the Columbia bridge which was the longest covered bridge in the world, being over a mile long. Union troops first tried to blow up the bridge, but when this did not work they set it on fire to stop the advance of the Confederates. On the return march, some tarried at the house of the widow Camble at Classley to partake of a peace offering of doughnuts and cakes meant for the dreaded Rebel cavalry.

Confederate prisoners taken at Gettysburg were quartered at the Paoli parade grounds and helped gather the harvest. One “Cracker” veteran remarked that in Pickett’s charge he found himself standing alone, “like a fool,” so he threw up his hands and surrendered.

The outrageous treatment of prisoners of war by the Confederate authorities was the occasion of the “waving of the bloody shirt” in after years. As a local member of McCall Grand Army Post remarked to a reconstructed ‘Greyback’ at a reunion of the Blue and Grey at Gettysburg. &ldI can forgive you for everything except the way you treated your prisoners” “Friend!” replied the ’Cracker, “We-uns would not have treated you-uns that-away. It was shirkers at home, who never saw a battlefield.”

Among the prisoners released from that awful slaughter pen at Andersonville, Georgia, there was one who returned to the little tenant house of John Rees on the OLd Lancaster road, to die in a few weeks. He was reported to have been in the most pitiful condition, a mere skeleton from vermin, disease, and stavation. Another was Jonathan Smiley, Company A, 8th Pennsylvania Cavalry, of Howellville, prisoner for almost a year, he lived to be almost the last survivor.

James A. Cornett, Company F, 5th Pennsylvania Cavalry, captired when he had almost served his entitlement, was confined at Andersonville, Georgia , and Florence, South Carolina for several months. He was exchanged, brought home to die April 29, 1865, and buried at St Peter’s.

During Lincoln’s second campaign for the Presidency, Easttown has marching clubs, or “Wideawakes” as they were called. The ranks were filled with returning soldiers whose perfect alignment was the pride of their partisians, and they carried with the stars and stripes at the head of the line a beautiful banner presented by the patriotic ladies of the township.

When Benjamin Harrison, a few years later, conducted his successsful presidential campaign, Easttown had probably the largest and best drilled club of the times, and in the midst of the campaign, the leaders, mostly men who were ignorant of local tradition, suggested that the name of the club be changed to Berwyn, since few people outside of the county knew where Easttown was situated. D. Bernard Stout, an old soldier and resident of Waterloo Mills, arose in meeting and made an impassioned speech against this, he pointed to the old banner on the platform, still borne at the head of the line, inscribed with the name of Easttown, and recited its history with rough eloquence. When he sat down there was an impressive silence for the space of a few minutes and nothing further was said of changing the name of the club.

Area farmers in Colonial times returned more than a score of Negro slaves in local tax rolls, the descendants of these and of some acquired probably via the “underground” route as cheap farm labor, had squatted mostly in wooded folds in the hills, and up to the Civil was formed a very small percentage of the population.

With freedom came a hegira northward of Negro families fresh from the towns and plantations of the south, bearing all the humility of a long subdued race. Being inoffensive and somewhat irresponsible they gave no cause for personal violence from the irreconcilables and even had the latter been disposed to interfere, the new comers had the protection of the so-called “Black Republicans.”

Among the local arrivals was a deep-chested old man, Tommy Ross. His sons cam with him. Ben had belonged to a black regiment and had been wounded in the leg in the assault at Pettersburg, under Burnside. When the surgeon decided to amputate. Bem was so scared that he crawled out of the hospital where he saw arms and legs piled up like cord wood, and hid in the woods. When they found him the next day his leg was so much better they decided to save it, in consequence it served him well for nearly half a century more. He later deserted to join another regiment, and it was under the name Isaacs that he received a pension. He worked in Reeseville, later Berwyn, for 16 years as a mason tender, gradually learning the trade which he followed in after years.
