Chapter 10: Rising of the Automobile Age

1901 - 1929

The average resident, if there ever is such a person, awoke on January 1, 1901, with little thought as to the changes a new century would bring. Much later, historians concluded that the passing of the frontier in America had already taken place in 1893, and some significant forces of change were at work in the nation. 

The center of population had moved west to southern Indiana and would continue to move toward the Pacific coast as each successive U.S. Census in the new century was recorded. Migration, nourished by mobility, was under way. 

A manner of some importance to the Pennsylvania Railroad at this time was assuring a sufficient water supply for existing and future needs of its steam locomotives.The company had perfected the technique of picking up water from troughs alongside the trackson the fly and installed this equipment along its main line at St. David’s and Glen Loch. The railroad retained American Pipe Manufacturing Company of Philadelphia to develop a distribution network for the sites, utilizing the Pickering creek water supply.

On July 23,1895, officials of the American Pipe incorporated the water companies: Easttown Water Company; Tredyffrin Water Company; Villanova Water Company, serving Radnor township; Willistown Water Company; and East Whiteland Water Company. One week later, Easttown Water was renamed Berwyn Water Company and it acquired the other four companies. 

During its four years of existence, Berwyn Water developed the Pickering creek pumping station near Phoenixville and built the Diamond Rock reservoir at the highest point on the line into the Valley. It had also laid pipes along Lancaster turnpike from Bryn Mawr to Glen Loch, providing public water to our local area. In 1899, North Springfield Water Company acquired Berwyn Water. The growing water industry, shared by many companies, was consolidated in 1925, when the community suppliers were acquired by Philadelphia Suburban Water Company.

Ice played an important role in the early days of the twentieth century, a time when fresh and perishable foods from other parts of the world became available, but electric refrigeration for homes was still in the future. Few homes in Berwyn had springhouses for cooling and storing food. The swinging shelves, usually found hanging from basement rafters, were at best unsatis-factory. The icebox was welcomed into the kitchen despite its drawbacks of emptying the drip pan or running out of ice at a crucial time.

The Berwyn Ice Company began operation October 7, 1901 on Lancaster pike at Woodside avenue. It advertised its product as “pure ice manufactured from pure spring water”	at the source of Darby creek,	old Springhouse tavern. The	plant was managed for about	two years by Charles Z. Jones	of Kromer avenue. Jones was	succeeded by George Turner	who took up residence at the south east corner of Berwyn	and Woodside avenues, a block	from the plant. 

Cash flow was a problem. The plant was mortgaged in 1906. When the company defaulted in 1913, Bryn Mawr Ice Company became the owner. Shortly after this the tall red-brick building used for ice storage was erected. It had the capacity to store two thousand tons of ice. The sign atop the building read, “Ice Never Fails,” and remained a Berwyn landmark for many years. But ice manufacturing finally did fail and its operations ceased around 1950. In 1971 the tall brick building and its sign came down. The long, low building which once housed horses, delivery wagons, and later trucks is today Yang’s Market.

A “Town Meeting” was held in the Odd Fellows Hall on October 3, 1905, at which about 125 “citizens and ladies” were present, to discuss and offer suggestions “for the improvement of Berwyn.” 

A number of suggestions were made, and, as reported in the Minutes of the meeting, “These suggestions took a tangible form in a motion ... that a Committee of 3 (later changed to 5) be appointed... to secure all information possible relative to improvements and to draw up a constitution and by-laws to form an Improvement Society whose object shall be to improve conditions in Berwyn.” The motion was passed by the meeting, and Henry 0. Garber, William Fritz, George Maxton, the Rev. R.N. Powers, and AM. Snider were appointed to constitute the committee.

Two weeks later the committee presented its report, and “after carefully considering and amending the same” it was accepted and adopted. It was then moved “that a permanent organization called the Berwyn Town Meeting be formed under the Constitution and By-Laws” that had just been approved. This too was approved, with 24 persons enrolled as charter members. (In the following March the name was changed from the Berwyn Town Meeting to the Berwyn Citizens’ Association.)

From the beginning, the establishment of a reading room and library was the major project of the organization. At the same time, the extension of street lights and sidewalks in Berwyn and the disposal of garbage were also areas of improvement to which attention was given.

At the meeting of October 3, 1905, a committee of five was appointed to inquire further into conditions, sites, etc., for a new library. This committee reported the following at the second Town Meeting: All attempts must be on a modest basis; other near-by libraries had reported very small beginnings and meager interest; at least $500 would be needed a year, and they suggested means of obtaining this money.

At the November 16 meeting the Reading Room Committee was instructed to secure a room for six months with the privilege of extending the time to one year. By January 1906 the minutes show the Reading Room in operation on the upper floor of what was then “The Bakery” on Waterloo avenue and a Special Committee was appointed to purchase tables and games, these in addition to magazines and papers already subscribed for.

About this time evidently the Committee was greatly enlarged. The additional names were 16 in number. Mr. William Fritz and Mr. George Hutton were largely responsible for financial support. Members of the Committee shared the work of a Librarian. A Special Committee headed by Mr. Coates examined all books offered or secured for the Libraiy. By March 1906 the Committee requested that its quorum be lowered to but eight members.

An invitation was extended to the Women’s Auxiliaiy of the Chester County Hospital to use the room for its monthly meetings. Minutes likewise report that a loan of 50 books had been made by the Friends Library of Philadelphia. Books had also been loaned by the State Library at Harrisburg.

There was need for a Librarian. Mrs. Elsie Jardine was appointed in November of 1906. In 1910 the Library moved to the Yerkes Building on Lancaster Pike. Here the first book stacks were built. Money was raised by “candy made and sold by the members.” The shelves were built by Mr. J.P. Lamborn. A standard system of cataloging was also installed and the Committee spent many long hours in cataloging all the books. Townspeople worked unceasingly that the Library might succeed, and it today is the result of the untiring efforts of many citizens. (The Reading Room/Library then established, incidentally, later became what we know as the present-day Easttown Library and Information Center.)

Berwyn’s largest manufacturing enterprise,	the American Bronze Company (later	reorganized under various names, the last	of which was American Non-Gran Bronze	Company) operated between 1907 and 1959 in the building known	today as the Bronze Building. It produced castings of a	special bronze alloy which	were machined into bushings	and bearings used in	automobile and aviation	engines. The technology	employed was contributed by	Englishman Alfred Hodgson Smith, a metallurgist	who had worked out and brought to this country	with him an idea for a special type of alloy. (Smith,	by the way, was over 65-years of age when he came here to pioneer the new company. He died at his home in Berwyn in 1919.) Jack Watson, of Wayne, handled administrative matters and was the financial backer.

The new company grew rapidly. Within two years the original foundry building was enlarged, the number of furnaces and employees was increased and more lathes were added to the production line. By 1912 the quarters were outgrown again, and a new modern foundry with a “saw-toothed” roof for maximum lighting and ventilation was erected. This was the period of immigration to America from southern and eastern Europe. Brothers Henry and Fernando Toroni came from Italy to Berwyn and worked at the “Bronze.” Both made their homes here and held important supervisory posts in the plant. In the beginning the products were used by automobile and truck manufacturers. During the first World War, every truck sent overseas was equipped with a kit of bronze bushing material for emergency field repairs.

Later the company began to work in the aviation field, providing bushings for Pratt & Whitney engines. Bushings from the Berwyn plant were said to be in the Wright engine that powered Charles Lindbergh’s “Spirit of St. Louis” on its historic non-stop trans-Atlantic flight in 1927, one of the great achievements of the twentieth century. 

The picture post card craze in the United States was at its peak during the period 1905-1912. Especially appealing were real photo post cards showing images made by a local photographer. Berwyn had such a photographer. She was Miss Lucy Sampson who lived on Francis avenue with her sister, Sarah, and her sister’s husband. 

Lucy Sampson took numerous photographs of Berwyn and the adjacent Main Line area and had a most extensive collection of picturesque rural and sylvan scenes, historic buildings, interiors of stately homes, and group and individual portraits. Some of her work can still be found at post card shows, auction sales, and flea markets.

During the first decade of the century the deaths of three of Easttown’s most respected citizens were recorded. They were: Joseph W Sharp (1828-1908), who established his country estate, “Hawthorne,” near Leopard upon the death of his father in 1856 and was instrumental in organizing the Berwyn bank; Preston W. Lobb (1844-1903), who managed the Fritz lumber yard for many years and had an important role in the founding of the First Baptist Church of Berwyn; and William H. Burns (1856-1910), the proprietor of the Berwyn Planing Mill and builder of homes and many larger public buildings such as schools, churches, railroad stations, and business houses.

In 1907, the Pennsylvania General Assembly passed a supplement to its earlier acts governing high schools, which gave two or more adjoining townships the right to erect and keep joint high schools. On May 23, 1907, a joint meeting of the school boards representing Easttown and Tredyffrin townships was held in the Easttown High School building on Bridge avenue “to consider the advisability of uniting the two townships in high school work.”

Members of the Devon Citizens’ Association attending the meeting asked for time to hold a meeting of their own to discuss having a joint high school as they were not sure that this was the thing to do.

George Hutton was elected temporary chairman of this first Joint School Board in the state of Pennsylvania. A joint committee (J.H. Dingee, JP Lamborn, HR. Wilson, and George Johnson) was appointed to investigate and confer in the matter of grounds and building.

On June 6, 1907, the report of the committee was received and the committee continued. On June 26, D. Knickerbacker Boyd was selected as the architect and a town meeting called to present the proposal to the taxpayers at the Easttown High School building. On July 11 the meeting was held but no test vote was taken. The sentiment of the meeting was favorable. A total of 26 attended. A Devon Citizens’ Association member asked for a meeting where they could hear more from the Easttown Board.

On August 3, the Boards voted to buy John Beadle’s ground (on the southwest comer of Conestoga and Howellville roads, across the street from the North Berwyn school) and moved that the Committee get an option for 60 days at $4500. The Committee reported on August 16 that they could secure 3-1/4 acres of the Beadle ground of $5000. All Directors except Thomas voted yes. William H. Burns was the successful bidder at $27,835 to build the school, with an additional cost of $3590 for heating. On December 19, 1908, the building was deemed completed. Formal dedication took place on February 9, 1909, in a snowstorm, with 300 persons present.

The 1909	enrollment of the	school was 72	students; this grew to 107 by 1920, and 330 by 1930. The school closed its doors on June 15, 1955(it was demolished in 1970),superceded by the construction of Conestoga High School, with an enrollment of 479 in the three High School classes. The first principal of the joint Tredyffrin-Easttown High School was Hayes C. Taylor, of Kennett Square

New homes continued to be constructed in Easttown. One of Devon’s most exquisite country houses, “Grey Craig,” was built in 1902 for James W. Patterson along Waterloo road about a mile and a quarter from Devon station. Designed by architect William Price, the English Tudor house was erected at the crest of the hill (450 feet elevation) overlooking 76 acres.

Another new estate was Philadelphia attorney William C. Bullitt's 15-acre “Oxmoor” (named after the ancestral home near Louisville), south of Exeter road and west of Waterloo. One of his sons, William jr., was the first ambassador to the Soviet after it was recognized in 1933, while the other, Orville, was one of the founders of the local Blue Cross and chairman of the board of the Philadelphia Orchestra. Oxmoor today is known as “Rosedon” but is still a landmark Devon address. 

George Wharton Pepper, Philadelphia lawyer, threw in his lot with Easttown when he decided to become a resident. He tells the story in his autobiography, “The choice lay between a small tract of high-priced land near a railroad station and a large tract in the more remote farming area. We decided in favor of a farm, and in August of 1907 bought ... a beautiful tract of farmland and woodland. The tract comprised 177 acres. The property had once belonged to the sisters of General Anthony Wayne, and we were glad to find his signature as an attesting witness to one of the old deeds.” Pepper continued, “Upon the land there stood a stone farmhouse somewhat more than a hundred years old. There was a stream running though the property; and as foxes -	as well as other small game -were plentiful, we named the stream Fox Creek and to the place itself we gave the name Fox Creek Farm.”

An elaborate country house named “Kelso” after a family ancestor, constructed about 1907 off Berwyn-Paoli road was the summer home of Philadelphia investment banker, J. Gardner Cassatt. As early as 1860 the 124-acres had been the Jonathan T. Morris farm. Yes, it is likely that artist sister Mary Cassatt on a visit to Philadelphia at Christmas 1908 did get to see the new house. It is now the Upper Main Line YMCA.

The Devon Horse Show resumed in 1910, after a nine-year hiatus. The president of the Association then was John T. Windrim, architect, who had built an exquisite home in Devon at the corner of Sugartown and Fairfield roads, with J. Gardner Cassatt, of Kelso Farm in Daylesford, the vice president. Much of the credit for the success of the revival of the Devon Horse Show, however, is usually given to the untiring efforts of William T. Hunter, who owned a small farm near the grounds and was treasurer of the Association.

When the show resumed in 1910 it was, as one writer described it, “already large” and “veering from rusticity to brilliance." (This is reflected in the composition of the Board of Governors and their selection of honorary vice presidents of the Association. Among the honorary vice presidents, for example, were Philander C. Knox, Charles Custis Harrison, Charles Lea, Dr. Charles B. Penrose, George Wharton Pepper, and Edward T. Stotesbury, while William C. Bullitt, Victor Charles Mather, A.]. Drexel Paul, M.A. Rosengarten, Welsh Strawbridge, and William Wayne were among the 32 members of the Board of Governors. Only D.B. Sharp, E.W. Twaddell, and Henry M. Warren were holdovers from the group that originally formed the Devon Horse Show Association in 1896). For the first time, the show was held over the Decoration Day (or Memorial Day) week end, a now three-day event on May 30th, and 31st and June 1st.

In 1913 William T. Hunter became chairman of the show, and in the following year it attracted more than 1000 entries and was described as “the largest outdoor show in the United States, and very probably in the world.” Its success has continued to build over the years. It is without doubt Easttown township’s preeminent sporting event.

The automobile had established itself as an economic force to be reckoned with. Automobile production in the United States since 1900 surpassed an aggregate of 1 million cars (statistics show 450,000 registered automobiles in 1912), but there were only 2.5 million miles of roads, most of them in towns and cities. Paving, if any, ended at the town line.

At this point Carl Fisher got involved. (He had already made a fortune by building the Indianapolis Motor Speedway and heading a company that made improved auto headlights.) Fisher went to a map and drew a straight line from New York to San Francisco, and declared that he would spearhead the construction of America’s first transcontinental highway. Fisher, an idea man who left details to others, was fortunate to attract as contributors two men influential in the world of car manufacturing: Frank A. Seiberling, president of Goodyear and Henry B. Joy, president of the Packard Motor Car Company.

On July 1, 1913, the road was officially named the Lincoln highway, and the Lincoln Highway Association was born. Joy was elected president of the association while Fisher, already elected vice president, was on a cross-country survey tour. In August, Henry Joy sketched out the chosen route for the Lincoln highway. In the East, a number of existing turnpikes were folded into the route, including the 63-mile stretch of the Philadelphia and Lancaster turnpike passing through Devon and Berwyn. Thus did the name “Lincoln Highway” come to be associated with our main street. (It was not until 1917 that the turnpike tolls were removed, and in 1925 Federal and state lawmakers voted to institute a new highway numbering system that meant the end of named highways. U.S. Route 30 came into being, but the name Lincoln highway did not easily go away.)

Henry Oscar Garber, a Schuylkill county native born in 1862, learned telegraphy and as a young man worked for the Pennsylvania Railroad a brief time in Berwyn. After marriage and starting a family, he returned to Berwyn in 1893. There he opened a newsstand and general store on the Lancaster turnpike just west of Waterloo avenue. He added an eastern section to it, so that the two-room storeroom had an upper and lower level. The store was a neighborhood meeting place where men sat around the stove and spun their yarns.

An ardent sportsman, Henry Garber had a keen interest in hunting and fishing. He kept a horse for fox-hunting and seldom turned down a hunting trip to Camp Lamoka, near Monroeton, for deer. Anyone who got a deer would hang it from the rafters in front of the store, and in the fall there might be several deer hanging there. His son-in-law was a local butcher.

During the years of the bicycle, Garber made runs to Atlantic City and was considered one of the finest amateur riders on the Main Line. He also took an active interest in the local baseball teams during the early days of the Main Line League.

Ever active in community affairs, he was a charter member of the Berwyn Fire Company, a Republican county committeeman for a number of years, a school director in Easttown township, and postmaster in Berwyn for ten years, from 1904 to 1913. Theodore Roosevelt signed the documents commissioning him postmaster. He tended his store to the very end and died on September 14, 1943.

Many stories exist as to who owned the earliest automobiles used in our area. Henry Garber was identified by his grandson Henry Pyle some years ago as having the first automobile in Berwyn, date not specified, a Cadillac. A newspaper reported in 1910 Garber had purchased a new Mitchell touring car. Mr. Pepper, in his book, says his place was more than four miles from Devon and in 1907 an automobile became a necessity. Charles Z. Jones, owner of the Berwyn Plumbing & Heating Company has been named by George Roberts as having had one of the first Model T’s (they came out in 1908), and C.C. Wilson’s first car was a 1905 Maxwell, according to his son Dave.

In later days, probably the 1920s, Berwyn had two garages - Fell’s, across from the Fritz lumber yard, a Buick agency, and Bill Trowill’s, at the other end of town, across from the primary school. (Who could have predicted then today’s strip of auto dealerships stretching from Devon to Berwyn: BMW, Mercedes, Jeep, Saturn, Toyota, Nissan, and Volvo.)

Although the automobile was making great strides, it was still in its infancy. The Pennsylvania Railroad continued to enhance its service and earn public good will. From the time the railroad rebuilt its line in 1877, it was said, four tracks came into Berwyn, and only three went on to Paoli. With the growth of the suburban commuters and commuter trains in the early 1900s ( there were 60 trains daily on the Main Line alone), the problem of handling the passenger traffic in and out of Broad Street station in Philadelphia became acute.

Following a study, in March 1913 the railroad announced plans to electrify the Main Line service for suburban traffic between Philadelphia and Paoli. The project included the construction of overhead wires and cables called a catenary. A by-product of electrification was the installation of light-position signals to replace the semaphore arms formerly used for signaling. Electrified operation was begun on September 11, 1915. The suburban terminus and yards of the railroad then gravitated to Paoli, and Berwyn was left, more or less, behind.

The European war which had commenced in August of 1914 grew ever more ominous. President Woodrow Wilson and the United States maintained a posture of strict neutrality. The announcement in January 1917 that the German navy would engage in unrestricted submarine warfare against all shipping to Great Britain prompted Wilson to break off diplomatic relations. The sinking of American ships led to a U.S. declaration of war early in April 1917. A Selective Service Act followed which made all men between the ages of 21 and 31 eligible for the draft. More than four million U.S. men were under arms when the conflict ended in 1918; U.S. deaths from all causes, including flu, totaled 112,000.

The names of local residents who served are preserved on the stone memorial put in place by the community next to the 16th milestone on Lancaster avenue (opposite the intersection of Waterloo road) on the second anniversary of the Armistice, November 11, 1920. The bronze plaque reads, “World War, 1917-1918, in honor of the men of Easttown and Tredyffrin Townships who answered their country’s call.” Inscribed are the names of 304 men (including four overseas workers). The names of nine men killed in action or who died of disease are marked with a star. They made the supreme sacrifice:

Thos. Levering Bolster

Chas. J. Kramer

Carmiene Capuzza

Lewis G. Smith

LeRoy Dalton

Walter H. Walker

Everett Henry

Christian Wanzel

Edgar Weaver



The memorial, moved several times over the years, now stands on Lancaster avenue at the southern entrance to the new pedestrian way bridging the railroad tracks at the train station, called by some the new Berwyn town center.

Franklin Lorenzo Burns, known locally in Easttown township as “Frank Burns”, was a well known and highly respected ornithologist and	local historian. He authored	“The Ornithology of Chester	County, Pennsylvania,” a book	published in 1919, and later	in his career was a charter	member (1936), president,	and publication editor	of the Tredyffrin Easttown	History Club.	

According to his own written	record, Frank Burns was born at Sharp’s Corner in Easttown in 1868. His father built a house in North Berwyn for the family on the Old (Conestoga) road in 1876, and thereafter it would be Frank Burns' home until his death February 7, 1946. He chose painting as his career (an older brother, W.H. Burns, was an important building contractor), and for many years he was one of the prominent house and construction painters of the Main Line, having many men in his employ and accepting large contracts.

As a boy, his father instilled in him his own interest in nature and in local history, and from his youth Frank Burns began to collect data and specimens and to make notes on both these subjects. He was a great student of the birds of Chester county and of bird migrations. His ornithological records began in 1884 and his record of seasonal bird migrations began the following year. Later he often remarked that he had the longest record of bird migration reports being made to the Smithsonian Institution; this report record extended over sixty years. He had a little square house by his residence, near the street, where children curiously peeked in to see his collection of mounted birds and trays of eggs.

As he aged, his interests turned more toward local history, although through his life he had collected all available data on the subject, both from published books, local records, and informants' statements. Everything that he heard he wrote down. This information formed the basis for his many articles published in the Quarterly of the local history club and in the Picket Post, the publication of the Valley Forge Historical Society. He bequeathed a rich legacy of local history to us, indeed.

Frank Burns was also involved in the Berwyn Fire Company which took a long step forward when it dedicated a new fire house and community hall on May 8, 1929, at 23 Bridge avenue. Newspaper accounts of the dedication state that it was a “red letter day” in the history of Berwyn. William Fritz presented the key to Frank Burns and Frank F. Walker. Edward J. Redmond, Commander of Dalton-Wanzel Post of the American Legion, presented and dedicated a flag and flagpole. It is said the ladies of the auxiliary earned and gave the sum of $14,000 toward the building of the fire house.

The old fire house had been located around the corner on Berwyn avenue in a small structure erected soon after the company organized. Dr. James Aiken was president and Temple Gregg, secretary, when the first motorized equipment was acquired in 1917. That was the year the Ladies Auxiliary organized, to help raise funds for that first American La France engine.

Berwyn churches also moved forward when, encouraged by pastor Rev. Thomas J. Aiken, Trinity Presbyterian Church sponsored a mission Sabbath School in Paoli. The first exercises were held on July 2, 1892 in a building rented from Henry Schofield on the north side of Lancaster pike west of what is now Route 252. In time, a site on Darby road was secured, a Chapel was erected by Ottmer Palmer, a local contractor, and numbers grew sufficient to organize a church on October 26, 1899. Twenty-three founding members signed the charter; sixteen of them had been members in Berwyn given letters of transfer by Trinity Church.

On April 1, 1901, Rev. Aiken, twenty-two years pastor at Trinity, was called to the newly organized Paoli church, having been released with regret by the congregation in Berwyn. The Rev. Robert N. Powers accepted a call to Trinity. He was installed on December 10, 1901 and stayed until 1908. During the Powers pastorate the mortgage debt on the newly constructed Berwyn church building was completely repaid.

The tenure of the young Rev Dr. W. Potter Van Tries spanned the years 1908 to 1911. He resigned his pastorate, married Daisy Aiken, a niece of former pastor T.J. Aiken, on December 28, 1911, and accepted a call to a Presbyterian church in Altoona. Near the end of his career, he retired to Berwyn and preached on occasion at Trinity. On June 30, 1957, he preached his 50th anniversary sermon and died shortly thereafter.

Long pastorates were in vogue during the early years of the twentieth century. The Rev. Dr. J. Charles Levengood preached at Trinity Church in Berwyn from 1912 to September 30, 1940. The son of a Honey Brook doctor, he was dearly loved by the congregation. In 1929 he arranged to move the church cemetery to free up space for future building and obtained the necessary decree of Chester County court. Building plans and the cemetery move were delayed, however, by the depression and World War II.

Baptist Church in the Great Valley: The church continued in a quiet way during the long pastorate of the Rev. Dr. Joseph Evans Sagebeer, 1904-1926. He had a Ph.D. in psychology and was the son of the Rev. William Sagebeer who served at the Newtown Baptist church for many years.

The old church with a great past celebrated its bicen-tennial June 1, 1911. It was then the abode of the dead. One speaker, Dr. George Morris Phillips, of West Chester State Normal School (now West Chester University) stated that he had walked through the churchyard and observed the tombs of his grandparents, two great-grand-parents, two great-great-grandparents, and four great-great-great-grandparents. Letters were read from descendants of some of the former pastors and reference was made to ever faithful elders, deacons, and mission-aries, whose bones had long since mouldered away in the, at this period, best kept cemetery in the two townships.

The First Baptist Church: Rev. Fryer resigned November 30, 1904, and the Rev. Esco! S. Sellers, estimator for an engraving firm in Philadelphia, supplied until he was ordained as pastor on June 29, 1905. During Pastor Sellers’ leadership, the church debt was liquidated. He remained until March 1917 and was followed by the Rev. Herbert Hargrave, 1917-1921; the Rev. John G. Booker, former pastor of the Baptist Church in the Great Valley, 1922-1925; the Rev. George O. Read, 1925-1927; and the Rev. Franklyn W Wiley, a student from Eastern Baptist Theological Seminary, 1927-1935.

During Sellers’ pastorate the membership increased to 150 members, but later there seemed to be a distinct trend toward the mother church, the Chapel gaining ground. Wiley’s personality, however, consolidated those remaining into a compact and distinct organization holding much to themselves. Up until Rev. Read’s pastorate the congregation had sponsored numerous benefits, suppers, and festivals, but in January, 1925, it was decided that all money should come through direct sacrifice of the donor.

Berwyn Methodist Church: The Rev. Alden W Quimby, 1896-1922, has been characterized by a history writer as a “gentle and kindly” pastor. His commitment to his ministry was deep, and he always gave it his first priority. He was, however, an exceptional	individual. He enjoyed taking long walks	in the surrounding countryside, and was	well known to residents for miles	around Berwyn because of his frequent	expeditions on foot. His interest in	history eventually led him to write an historical novel about Valley Forge. As	an amateur astronomer, he was an active	observer of the sun for over thirty-two years,	and he willingly shared his love of astronomy with others. Rev. Quimby died on September 23, 1922 at age 66. The next year the church's pipe organ was dedicated as a memorial to him.

In conformity with Methodist custom, local pastors were changed by the Conference every few years. Following Quimby, the Rev. J.C. Tenant served as supply May 1922 to January 1923; then the Rev. Paul W. Poley, 1923-1925; the Rev. J. Carpenter Zook, 1925-1927; and the Rev. Frank Mack, 1927-1929.

St. Monica Roman Catholic Church: Father John Carey was assigned to the parish in 1906. During his tenure, the parish built a school, purchased a house to remodel as a convent, and stuccoed the wooden church exterior. The old horse sheds were taken down about 1917. Chester County Historical Society preserves to this day a bill receipted in Father Carey’s hand for “$6.00 rent of horse stable to Mr. W. W. Hoopes” dated April 16, 1911.

On September 8, 1916, the parish school was formally opened with three nuns who traveled each day from Immaculata College (now University) and taught in the church basement until the school was completed, March 19, 1917. Nine years later a house adjacent to the church property was purchased from the Armstrong family, and on March 19, 1926 nuns took up residence for the first time in the parish.

Father Carey died on November 6, 1939, a few days after his seventy-fifth birthday, having been pastor of St. Monica parish for thirty-three years.

St. David’s Episcopal Church: During the latter year of Rev. Keller's term he had been assisted by the Rev. James Hart Lamb, D.D., and at the Easter meeting of the congregation following Mr. Keller's death, Dr. Lamb was unanimously chosen as rector of the church. He began his ministry on Sunday, April 6, 1902.

Dr. Lamb presided over the commemorative exercises celebrating the Bicentenary of St. David's Church held on September 4-5, 1915. He was succeeded by the Rev. Crosswell McBee, 1922-1945.

The automobile, no doubt, brought an end to the days of the glorious Devon Inn. In April 1914 owners John W and Ellen Simmons Patten sold the Inn and about 14 acres of ground. For a while the building was occupied by the Devon Manor School for Girls. In 1926 it reopened as the Devon Park Hotel for two years, and after remodeling, it became the Valley Forge Military Academy with Captain Milton Baker as the superintendent, a staff of thirteen, and 117 cadets. A few months later, on January 18, 1929, a disastrous fire swept through the old building and totally destroyed it. The famous and well-known landmark, the old Devon Inn, was no more.

Chapter 11: Depression, Defense, and Development

1930 - 1964

Our local history writers have recorded little of their recollections of the “great depression” which afflicted the decade of the 1930s. Perhaps the memories are still too vivid, too painful, or too distressing to describe. 

Writers on a broader scale have left some facts to ponder. Gifford Pinchot entered into his second term as Pennsylvania's governor in 1931 and was faced by hard times and an increase of unemployment to alarming proportions. The state had only eight per cent of the population of the United States but had ten per cent of the unemployed. Agriculture was similarly affected. Farm prices, over the decade from 1919 to 1929, had dropped more than 50%, and then from 1929 to 1932, sixty per cent more. The farms of Easttown would never again meaningfully supply crops and foodstuffs for the marketplace. 

Franklin Roosevelt, newly elected president of the United States, quickly acted to shore up the banking system. Two days after his inauguration, he issued a proclamation on March 6, 1933, closing all banks until Congress could meet in special session. (Berwyn National Bank just three years earlier had embarked on a building program to enlarge and renovate its facilities on Lancaster avenue in accordance with plans and specifications prepared by Ritter and Shay, Architects. The project was completed in October of 1930). The bank was closed from March 10, 1933 until February 8, 1934, but no money was lost by depositors. In October of 1934 the death of William H. Doyle, a director, was noted by the bank Directors in a tribute in appreciation for his services both to the bank and the community, especially during the period of suspended banking services.

Any employment opportunity was greatly esteemed. A highway project which will resonate clearly with today’s Easttown residents, widening of Lancaster avenue through Berwyn, commenced about 1930. Pavement was extended from Grove avenue in Strafford, south of the railroad, to connect with Lancaster avenue in Berwyn (prior to this time the street we know as “Old Lancaster” north of the railroad was the only thorofare available). Then in April of 1931 the newspaper reported, “Berwyn property owners, as well as the Chester County Commissioners, are anxiously awaiting word from the State Highway Department as to the latest decision on plans for the widening of [Lancaster avenue] through town.	The original plan	would have resulted in the razing and altering of many business properties	and would have caused thousand of dollars in damages which the county would have to pay...”

As it turned out, the construction greatly altered the grade of the highway as can be noted from references by local writers in the Quarterly. The Walker twins, Merle (Lee) and Mildred Oones), writing about the Berwyn Pharmacy say, “In early days, before Lancaster avenue was improved in the 1930s, the drug store sat high on the street. Five steps led up to the door, wider steps at the bottom and a second set of narrower steps at the entrance to the store.” Also, Sara B. Nuzum writing about Cook's store (later Beadle’s, still later Williams’) at Lancaster and Bridge avenues says, “In 1930 the Turnpike was changed to four lanes. They took the porch off the store, and at that time Harry Williams remodeled and stayed in business until his death in 1941.”

The school authorities in Easttown decided to upgrade	the elementary school facilities early in 1930. They acquired a tract of land on the south side of First avenue, east of Bridge avenue, in Berwyn, from the Coates family, hired architects, and let bids for the construction of a new Easttown Elementary School. The new school was first occupied in the fall of 1932.

In 1933, the old Grammar School, previously closed in 1926, was razed. The south room of the annex, Building No.2, became, for the next eight years, the site of the Berwyn Library. It was also used for many years as a meeting place for Easttown township supervisors until the new Township Building was built in 1958 on Berwyn avenue on the east side of town.

In 1932 the Paoii Branch of the American Red Cross relocated to the other room of the former schoolhouse. The outbreak of war in Europe in 1939 brought a great increase in Red Cross volunteer activities. Negotiations commenced with the Easttown School Board to purchase the building The transaction was completed in April of 1943, the library having moved out some months earlier to the Aiken building (old Berwyn Pharmacy) on Lancaster avenue. From the Red Cross and others, the building descended to become headquarters for Surrey Services for Seniors today.

Storm clouds of war were again building on the horizon in Europe. Then came the surprise Japanese attack on the U.S. Naval base at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941.

“The regimentation of the physical, mental, and spiritual entities of a people to the will of a single mind, however efficient to accomplish a set and determined purpose, cannot result in the lasting good or happiness of the world.” So stated the editor of our local history journal in the first edition published after the attack. The response on the home front was immediate.

On December 9th, orders came through for full time observation of the overflight of all aircraft. (The U.S. Army had conducted a series of tests for observation of planes in this area in October of 1941.) At 6 p.m. the Berwyn Observation Post started on twenty-four-hour duty. With no protection against the weather, and having to go down a long ladder to telephone messages, Clarence Reifsneider, who had established the Post on the High School roof for the earlier tests, looked for a more desirable location. The Road Supervisors of Tredyffrin township were approached and they agreed to build a place on the roof of the township building on Old Lancaster road, about half a mile southwest of the High School.

The Army was agreeable, and Walter Eaves, Mr. Leighton, and Mr. Waterworth, the Road Supervisors, started work for the new observation post. They had a doorway cut through the south wall of the building, and a stairway with a railing and a platform constructed on the roof.A former traffic watch-boxwith windows on three sides and a door with glass was placed on the platform. A telephone and electric line were put in place and on December 16th the Post officially opened on the roof of the township building. Orientation marks which could be seen while telephoning were painted on the upper and lower roofs.

On December 19th, Mr. Reifsneider had to resign due to his connection with Bell Telephone Company. F. Alfred Patton was approached about taking over the duties of Chief Observer, which he agreed to do and resigned as an Observer on the Sugartown Post.

The first week on the job was to complete thr roster so that an observer would serve only once a week. With two people on a two-hour tour that would require 168 people. Several persons were on more than one tour, and Mrs. Franklin Wandless was on three times a week. Two Assistant Chief Observers were appointed: Mrs. Edith Reifsneider, who took care of the daytime observers, and William Armstrong, who handled the nighttime tours. In placing people on a tour, friends, spare time, and type of work or business were considered, which in the end paid dividends, because at the time of deactivation 90 of the original people were still included among the 157 people on a week’s duty. The Post was never without at least one observer on duty. The only difficulty encountered with manning it was during February when colds kept people away.

A flag pole was erected by Berwyn Plumbing and Heating Company and a flag bought by the observers. Franklin Wandless made an appropriate weathervane, depicting two observers, following a plane, and placed it on the roof.

A red flash message was reported just before 3 p.m. on May 26, 1943, when a plane crashed during a heavy rain storm on the Percy Wilson estate at Devon, two miles east of the Post.

When the Army distributed Aircraft Warning Service arm bands, the observers wore them while on duty. Later, when the Wings, in the form of a pin, were issued, the observers felt that they really were a part of the Army Air Force. The Post was deactivated in October of 1943.

Easttown was not without other talents. A young man with great musical ability graduated from Tredyffrin-Easttown High School in the wartime Class of 1942. He was Elliot Lawrence Broza, later known professionally simply as Elliot Lawrence. His family moved in 1936 to a house on the north east corner of Fairfield and Sugartown roads in Devon, and he grew up there.

His father was general manager and program director for radio station WCAU in Philadelphia and also producer and director of its popular Children’s Hour program, broadcast on Sunday mornings. Music was a normal accompaniment of Elliot Broza’s everyday life. From the age of two, he was fascinated by the piano, but as he grew older he also played the saxophone.

After the family moved to Devon, he took piano lessons from Stanley Gray, the music director for the Tredyffrin-Easttown school system, also doubling on the clarinet. This was about the time that the “Band Busters” was organized. An eleven piece dance band, made up of children between eleven and fifteen years old, the band used the third floor of the Broza home in Devon as a rehearsal hall. The group not only played on the Children’s Hour program, but also at private parties, for which the young musicians were paid from a dollar and a half to three dollars each. In addition to playing piano, saxophone, and clarinet in the band, Elliot Broza was its business manager, arranging bookings and handling all the band’s correspondence.

With this background it was inevitable that as a student at Tredyffrin-Easttown High School, Elliot Broza would be involved in just about everything pertaining to music, both instrumental and vocal. And he was.

After graduating from T-E, Broza entered the University of Pennsylvania, completing his course in a war-accelerated program in three years. He immediately took over as musical director of station WCAU, where he put together what George T. Simon, music critic and editor of Metronome magazine, later described as “the greatest studio band in the country.” The band featured vocals by Rosalind Patton and Jack Hunter, played sweet music, and achieved great popularity with the Philadelphia listening audience.

By the early part of 1946, Lawrence (as he was by then known) took the band on the road, with dates at prestigious venues, radio remotes, and recording contracts. Unfortunately, in the 1950s musical tastes changed and the days of the big bands were numbered. “Elliot Lawrence, his Piano and his Orchestra” will always be remembered fondly. If he had been born ten years sooner, there is no telling what he would have achieved.

Even though he had been bedridden in his mother’s home on Central avenue in Berwyn for several years, during World War II Bob Goebel wanted to be a part of the war effort. The result was “a monthly newspaper, published by Berwyn men and women on the Home Front for the Berwyn men and women on the Fighting Fronts.” The first issue appeared in April 1943, and its publication continued on a monthly basis until May of 1946, by which time nearly all those who had served through the war had returned home again.

Robert F. Goebel was seriously crippled when a disease, generally termed as arthritis, set in about a year after he graduated from Tredyffrin-Easttown High School in 1933. After an unsuccessful operation he was confined to his room. He conceived the idea of a home town newspaper, to be sent to service personnel during the war. Since there was no such paper, he volunteered to head the task as editor; the communications were to come to him.

A great volunteer effort ensued (there were 24 names on the masthead for the final issue) and the product was well received. Contributions of equipment, supplies and cash flowed in. The paper metamorphosed from four mimeo-graphed pages to a new and larger, printed format. In fact, so well did the Berwyn Post become a hometown newspaper that many of the local residents wanted it delivered to them too. A special December 1944 Christmas issue reached fourteen pages. From an initial circulation of 130 the numbers climbed to 2500 copies by the end of the war, including a large number of copies circulated locally.

A special thank you was given to Bob Goebel on September 22, 1944 when he received the American Legion Citation. The award was made in recognition of his work as editor of the Post, and was presented by William H. Kohlmeyer, service officer, and Clarence L. Reifsneider, adjutant, on behalf of Dalton-Wanzel Post No. 646 of Paoli.

Less than nine months later Robert F. Goebel was dead, at the age of 30. In early June he went to the hospital for an operation, and two days later, on June 13, 1945, he passed away. To the very end he displayed the same cheerfulness and faith that helped him meet and rise above the physical handicap under which he had labored, since a football accident twelve years before.

The war in Europe had ended, but in the Pacific hostilities continued. There was never any question about the future of the newspaper. The staff closed ranks and kept on producing the Post “in tribute to his memory.” Not until its 38th issue, May of 1946, did publication cease.

Fittingly, on the front page of the final issue was reproduced the program for the annual Memorial Day Service in Berwyn, to be held at 11 o’clock in the morning on May 30th at the Easttown Grammar School. A highlight of the service was the dedication, by Bill Pyott, assisted by members of Berwyn Girls’ Club, of a memorial plaque to honor Robert F. Goebel, to be placed in the Easttown Library.

Also, at the service, Dan Redman paid tribute to the Gold Star Veterans of World War II. A page in the last issue of the Post recognized twelve of them:

Thomas Armstrong

John Bartosh

Anthony Borzillo

Stephen Brooks

Daniel Connor jr.

Maurice S. Houston

Thomas E. Parlaman

Warren Phelps

Curtis K. Ritter

Alvin Stauffer

James D. Sweeney

John Carl Wright

No complete list is known to exist. A local committee for the erection of the Berwyn Veterans’ Monument is currently working on this. Likely the list eventually determined will be larger than that shown above.

For four days in June of 1952 the village, and most of adjoining Easttown and Tredyffrin with it, took time off to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the town named Berwyn. World War II had scattered close to 400 of its sons and daughters to the ends of the earth. With peace achieved, they returned with renewed pride in their home town to pick up the lose ends and seek a career. Many opted first for college and after four years, at graduation, found themselves faced with renewed armed conflict in Korea only weeks after receiving their degree. The feeling of patriotism, pride in nation and its accomplish-ments was at a high level, and everyone loved a parade.

Fourteen local organizations formed the sponsoring committee for the event. Paul L. Good was chosen general chairman, and veteran residents belonging to the community’s several organizations took up duties as committee chairmen and working members.

At noon on June 26 the fire whistle sounded the official opening of the celebration. All the buildings in town were decorated with flags and red, white, and blue bunting. Residents dressed up in old time costumes and special black derbies and top hats decorated with red bands. There was a hobby show open daily in the former Acme Markets building at the south west corner of Lancaster and Main avenues.

At 2 p.m. a memorial service at the monument on Lancaster avenue remembered deceased members of the community. In the evening at 6:30 p.m. there was a Little League baseball game between Berwyn and Devon-Strafford on the high school turf. The team uniforms were freshly washed and ironed for the occasion. A community church service and choir sing was held at the field following the game.

The next day, Friday, June 27, the Berwyn businessmen’s gala parade stepped off at 7 p.m. There were also ceremonies at the fire house following the parade to house the new 1000 gallon a minute Autocar pumper and burn the note on the new Cadillac ambulance.

Saturday, June 28 was set aside as Fireman’s Day. At 10:30 a.m. the annual meeting of the Chester County Firemen's Association convened in the fire house auditorium. After lunch, at 2 p.m. the firemen’s parade got under way featuring hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of equipment, with bands from far and near competing for prizes. It was a long parade on a hot day.

The celebration closed on June 29, with special worship services in the individual churches of Berwyn. On Sunday afternoon the results of the judging of vintage clothes worn during the week were announced. Charles Gibb took winning honors in the men’s division; Mrs. William Rambo in the women’s division; and Mr. and Mrs. Walter Brown were chosen the best dressed old-fashioned couple. It was, in short, a celebration not soon forgotten.

By 1952 even the youngest World War II veterans had completed their college courses. They were getting married, starting their careers, and the great “baby boom” had begun. Young families spent their weekends visiting sample houses.

Easttown Woods was Berwyn’s first post war housing development. Advertised as “surrounded by trees,” it offered homes at affordable prices just fifty years ago. The houses were appealing to new families. The location, of course, was superior, with the closeness of the Pennsylvania Railroad and the anticipation of the Schuylkill Expressway. And once on site, the young couple could appreciate the pains the architect and the builder, the Easttown Company, had taken to make an affordable home a truly fine place to live.

First, instead of following the usual method of clearing the land of all obstructions and laying out streets in grids, the builder left standing the large, medium-sized, and even small trees. Many of the homes were shaded by trees already fifty and seventy-five feet tall. On the southwestern side of Midland avenue Doyle & McDonnell once had their dogwood nursery. Homes there featured several full-grown dogwoods in their back yards.

The streets of the development curved and straightened in a pleasing way. Houses along the little branch of Darby creek sat low, while houses on the western side of Midland avenue sat high. The houses were also turned in different directions to avoid a “cracker box” look, and colors were in variety and selected by the architect. The salt box type was not a typical choice in Philadelphia’s suburban housing; more common at this time was the ranch house, and soon the rage would be the split-level.

Most Easttown Woods houses were built with only the first floor finished. On the first floor were the living room, dining room, efficiency kitchen, two bedrooms and bath. Utilities were in the basement. The living room featured a picture window. The dining room adjoined it with no separating wall, and the kitchen opened without doors or walls to the dining room. The effect was a brightness and spaciousness uncommon in a small house. 

Walter K. Durham, the architect, had considered the family who would be living in the home when he designed it. He gave remarkable attention to even small details. The open kitchen was equipped with an exhaust fan; the bathroom mirror was angled so that small members of the family could see themselves in it.

While the second floor was unfinished, it was ready for expansion. Most families set about immediately to complete it. The men worked together or alone; wives helped. Some families hired contractors to raise the back roof and put in a dormer and an upstairs bath. Those with houses with a garage also found that they could, after all, put a door from the garage into the basement, greatly improving accessibility to the house. Building a house is hard work, and few were experienced at it, but they learned from one another as they went along.

Most of the buyers were veterans and their families. The men were about 27 to 32 years old. Many were beginning professionals, teachers, accountants, an architect, and, the greatest in number, engineers. Most of them had one or two children when they moved in, and would have more; four children in the family would be common ten years hence.

It was a time of changing life style for the American family. Before the war a lifetime in the same community, with the extended family near by, was the common pattern. Now young couples set off on their own to distant places where there were no family ties. In Easttown Woods a number of people came from Michigan to work at the new Paoli center of the Burroughs Corporation; others came from western Pennsylvania and New York, in addition to those from other suburban Philadelphia areas.

The local residents, whose quiet little village these 75 new families also inhabited, were gracious and welcoming. It was a happy, supportive place to come to. Many of these newcomers had moved from city apartments where they had been met with indifference. The warmth of the village was immediately evident. Several widowed women, living with their families in the older part of town, became loving, capable baby-sitters.

Most of all, the newcomers supported each other. They were sharing a very happy time of their lives together; common interests bound them closely.

Home delivery men came regularly through the streets; breadmen, milkmen, an elderly gentleman who peddled his wife’s sticky buns on Tuesday and Saturdays, and eventually, the mailman. (During the first years of the development, when mail had to be called for at the post office, mothers trekked uptown with their strollers and walking toddlers. They “did the town” as they went along, and by the time the mail was home-delivered, the mothers and the town were well acquainted.)

The sidewalks on the west side of Midland avenue and the east side of Eastwood road at first saw heavy traffic in strollers, soon to be accompanied by tricycles and scooters. Back yards sprouted sand boxes and gym sets. Mothers gathered where the children were, to supervise.

The Easttown Board of Supervisors, in those early years, met at the Red Cross building behind the Acme, at Bridge and Lancaster avenues. The residents of Easttown Woods were well treated by the Supervisors; they did not always have their needs met, but they were always heard with courtesy. One of the gains they accomplished was to have a school crossing guard placed at the intersection of Waterloo and First avenues. When more of the children were in school, the township, the school district, and St. Monica Church cooperated in making safer paths, out of the roadway, for the children.

The shopping district was along Lancaster avenue, and the stores on the highway closed on Wednesday afternoons. They were managed primarily by long-time local residents. Mr. Day had a small drug store near the corner of Lancaster and Main avenues; when he retired in September of 1954 William Connor, of Kennett Square, moved in and became Berwyn’s pharmacist, soon expanding his store to the corner, buying the property from Josephine Latch. (Connor served the community 44 years until retirement in 1998.)

The Bridge Shop was just above the post office, and had a succession of owners; here were sold sodas, ice cream, snacks, and some groceries. Espenshade’s was a larger grocery store on the highway down near Midland avenue; they made deliveries back then. Across Main avenue from Connor’s was Harolds Department Store, managed for many years by the town’s most prominent Democrat, Lou Lieberman; his merchandise was fresh, of high quality, and well displayed, and included items in great demand by the families living in Easttown Woods, name brand women’s blouses, snow suits, polo shirts, and underwear for small children. A new hardware store opened, and soon had to expand.

These first few years were in many ways charmed ones for these new residents. Careers were moving ahead, and the growing mob of children was happy and healthy. In 1957 came the first recession, and with it a cutback at Burroughs that broke into the tranquil world of Easttown Woods. Over the next few years Burroughs was to lay off or transfer a number of employees.

New housing developments were springing up everywhere, yet the schools were remarkably adept at keeping ahead of the enrollment. In 1955 a wing with two kindergarten rooms and a cafeteria was added to the Easttown school. In 1957 the Devon school was ready and the Devon children were assigned there, and the Easttown school became known as the Berwyn school. In 1961 the new Hillside school took children from Berwyn who lived in the Bair road, Margo lane, Conestoga road area. In 1965 another group went off to the new Beaumont school.

New churches and church facilities also appeared. In October 1951, Trinity Presbyterian Church removed its cemetery from the corner of Berwyn and Waterloo avenues into the Great Valley Presbyterian churchyard in the Valley. On the Berwyn site it built an addition to the church including an auditorium seating 250, separate class rooms, a church kitchen and a pastor’s study, all completed in 1954. A new two-story education wing was dedicated in 1973.

First Church of Christ, Scientist, Berwyn, joined our community when it purchased the Chapel on Cassatt avenue near the railroad station from the Baptist Church in the Great Valley. The new congregation held its first service in the building on October 4, 1953.

Berwyn Methodist Church: The Rev. Stacy Myers began a twelve-year pastorate in May of 1953. During his tenure a 7-1/2 acre property was purchased from the Coates family, and the first buildings on the present church campus were consecrated in 1958. Three years later the original 1888 building on Main avenue was sold to Trinity Presbyterian church, leaving behind seventy years of fond memories. Rev. Myers was succeeded by the Rev. Harold Schieck in May of 1965.

St. Luke’s Evangelical Lutheran Church: After meeting for about a year in the old dance hall (Isabel E. Rogers Hall, Stone and Gables, Devereux School) in Devon, the Lutherans organized as a church on December 5, 1954. The Rev. Theodore Schlack was called as the first pastor. Land straddling the Easttown township line in Devon was purchased in 1955. The church met in the Red Cross Building in Berwyn while the church was being built. The first service in the newly constructed edifice in Devon took place on December 7, 1958.

Evangelical United Brethren: A church of Methodistic German background occupied a new building in 1962 on Darby Paoli road at Buttonwood. Not long after, in 1968, the denomination merged with the Methodist church to form the United Methodist church. The larger Berwyn church was the survivor locally. Today Congregation Or Shalom, a Jewish synagogue, occupies the location.

St. Norbert Roman Catholic Church: In 1956 a new parish began in Paoli, carved for the most part out of St. Monica in Berwyn, to relieve crowded conditions. The Norbertine fathers then resident at Daylesford Abbey were involved in opening the new location. The children of St. Norbert continued to use the school facilities of St. Monica until their own school building on Darby Paoli road was completed in early 1958. The first mass of St. Norbert parish was celebrated on June 18, 1956 in the Paoli Fire House.

St. Monica Roman Catholic Church: The Rev. John Driscoll was appointed pastor in January of 1957. He twice enlarged the school, the first expansion being in 1958, and built, the same year, a new convent, the old one having been torn down to enlarge the school. Father Driscoll died on September 6, 1968, at age 63.

Main Line Unitarian Church: Founded in 1958 by about twenty families in the area, the church found a permanent home in 1961 when it purchased the old Emory McMichael mansion on Valley Forge road near Maplewood, close to Old St. David’s church, in Devon. The Rev. Mason McGinness became the first pastor in 1963.

Work to organize a local YMCA began in 1962 and reached fruition when the Upper Main Line YMCA purchased the 54-acre Daylesford property of the Norbertine fathers on December 31, 1964. Originally part of the estate of J. Gardner Cassatt, the property includes a large brick mansion house and surrounding grounds which have been developed into a first-class YMCA.

The new Easttown Township building and adjoining Library, at the southwest corner of Lancaster and Midland avenues, opened in 1958. It was the first permanent home the township had. By then a number of the children in Easttown Woods were in school, and the library was a great convenience for them. A true dedication to educational excellence was apparent in the schools, and in the community at large.

At the end of five years, the first home owners in Easttown Woods began, in small numbers, to move out. By five years after that a good number had moved on, some transferred or promoted to another, distant city, others to larger homes nearby for their growing children. As a result, the community became more diverse. For some newcomers, it was a place to retire. But those who were early owners in Easttown Woods look back at those years and remember what a great place it was to start a family.

Issues of the Daily Local News published on March 20, 21, and 22, 1958 confirm what was doubtless a record snowfall for the area. The snow started during the day on the nineteenth. By early evening, traffic, even on the Lincoln highway, was virtually at a standstill. Police reported major tie-ups on both Route 30 and 202 (now Bear Hill road and the Paoli pike). The hill at Devon on the Lincoln highway, for many years a bottleneck when snow came, was completely blocked by stalled and abandoned cars and trucks. Emergency shelters had to be set up along Route 30 to provide food and sleeping accommodations for snowbound travelers, truck drivers, and marooned families.

By half past nine the following morning, the snow on the ground in West Chester was officially measured at 25 inches! Unofficial measurements in Paoli showed depths of as much as three feet. The unexpected storm surpassed all previously recorded snows, including the former all-time record storm of Christmas Day in 1909, officially measured at 21 inches, and the well-known Blizzard of 1888.

The snow was an extremely wet and heavy one, sticking to everything it fell on. Its weight coupled with high winds, resulted in many broken branches and fallen trees, causing thousands of families to be without electric power or telephone service and hampering road clearing and repair operations. Some were without service for three or four days, and in a few instances in the Great Valley for an even longer period of time. At the Philadelphia airport there were only four inches of snow recorded, but even that somehow seemed scarcely appropriate for the day before the first day of Spring.

That same year, Easttown lost its largest, and likely almost its last industry, when the American Non-Gran Bronze Company closed. During World War II the company employed close to 1000 workers on war production, operating on a three-shift, seven-day a week basis in several locations. After the war, the contracts were canceled and reorganization took place. New management modernized the plant and operated successfully until November of 1958, when a dispute over wages caused a costly strike lasting into the following year. Two months after the strike ended, the business was sold and its assets	and operations transferred to Chicago. Twenty-four trailer loads of equipment were moved from Berwyn.

The experiences of the homeowners in Easttown Woods were replicated countless times in countless developments in the following 50 years, in neighbor- hoods named Berwyn Downs, Country Estates, Dogwood Lane, Leopard Lakes, Lenape Farms, Beaumont, Devon Downs, and what seems to be an endless litany. In the twenty years from 1950 to 1970, the population of Easttown township grew from 3784 to 9565 bringing a huge need for support infrastructure of streets, sewers, trash (and leaf) removal, schools, library facilities, parks, and public safety. Incredibly, fire protection is still provided by our volunteer Berwyn Fire Company.
