Chapter 12: Recording Recent Events

1965 - 2003

The final third of the twentieth century was marked by continuing development in Easttown township. Happily, this time period also spans the incumbency of Gene Williams as township manager. He has held the position since 1977. 

An important factor in the township’s growth h without much space as been the 1980 revised zoning ordinance. The officials made a decision to zone most of its land as a bedroom community without much space for offices or businesses> The revisions helped to avoid “cookie cutter” development and promoted increased sensitivity to the environment and reduced litigation about subdivisions. The days of the small builder gave way to the likes of the luxury home builders of today. 

Easttown township is fortunate to be graced by many well maintained structures of historic note. Three of them have been protected by listing on the General Register of Historic Places. They are:

Historic Waynesborough, 2049 Waynesborough road, Paoli, listed March 7, 1973,

Roughwood, 107 Old Lancaster road, Devon, listed November 23, 1984

Waterloo Mills Historic District, Waterloo road, Devon, listed July 21, 1995 

Easttown township acquired title to the stone mansion house, “Historic Waynesborough,” birthplace of General Anthony Wayne, in 1980 from members of the Wayne family, after a successful fund-raising program conducted by the Committee to Preserve Waynesborough. The township leases the property to Philadelphia Society for the Preservation of Lanmarks which maintains and operates the house as a public museum.

Construction of a new Education and Visitor Center, an extension and renovation of the 1897 carriage house adjacent to the Wayne mansion took place during 2003. The addition provides space for archival storage of reference material on Anthony Wayne and his ancestral home. An upstairs area was designed as a library where formerly inaccessible documents can be made available to the public. It has been designated the Anthony Wayne Ridgeway Library, in memory of the late Tony Ridgeway, direct descendant of General Anthony Wayne.

“Roughwood” stands on the north side of what was once the Lancaster turnpike, opposite the intersection with Valley Forge road. It was named by Civil war Captain Albert Sidney Ashmead who purchased the house as a country residence in 1868. Built in 1805, it originally was The Lamb tavern licensed in 1812 by George Rees, a Revolutionary War hero who later served as sheriff of Philadelphia. It is today a private residence.

Waterloo Mills is significant as an example of an intact, agriculture-based, 19th century hamlet. It is historically important for its association with the milling industry and crop and dairy farming in the period 1798 to 1909. During much of this time the district functioned as a nearly self-contained farming and blacksmith community, containing the only gristmill in Easttown township. Tax records show the mill was in place by 1798. From 1853 to 1867 the mill also served as Easttown’s first post office. The village and surrounding 167 acres is today part of the Waterloo Mills Preserve along Darby creek owned by the Brandywine Conservancy, and Waterloo Mill has been renovated into living quarters.

In addition to sites listed on the National Register, Easttown homes have been featured six times by the Philadelphia Vassar Club on their annual Scholarship Fund “Show House and Gardens” tour event. The six historic and architecturally pleasing homes are a cross section of the best township streetscapes:

Grey Craig, 680 Wetherby lane, Devon, 1987

Rosedon, 500 Waterloo road, Devon, 1991 

D'Orsay, 100 South Devon avenue, Devon, 1992 

Hilltop, 570 Beaumont road, Devon, 1997

The Woods, 1560 Sugartown road, Paoli, 2001

Pennview, 630 Waterloo road, Devon, 2002 

A number of individuals who have lived or still live in Easttown homes have achieved recognition at the national level.

The late Thomas S. Gates jr., a native of Philadelphia but for many years a Devon resident, had a distinguished career as a naval officer, banker, and public servant. He was secretary of the navy and secretary of defense in the administration of President Dwight Eisenhower and ambassador to the People's Republic of China in the administration of Gerald Ford. The Navy, in 1988, named a newly commissioned guided missile cruiser the USS Thomas S. Gates in his honor.

Easttown has been enriched by the young couple who took up residence here about 1980. Both	of them also knew the White House as a	family home. David Eisenhower is the	grandson of President Dwight Eisenhower	and a son-in-law of President Richard Nixon. His wife Julie is the daughter of President Nixon. David is a professor at the University of Pennsylvania. Both are published authors. Both helped with fundraising for the new Easttown Library & Information Center prior to its construction. Their children, Jennie, Alex, and Melanie, attended Easttown schools.

Just fifty years ago, Miss Evelyn Ay of Ephrata, Miss Pennsylvania, competed in the annual pageant at Atlantic City and was crowned Miss America 1954. She was engaged to be married to Carl Sempier who was in the Navy flight school preparing to be an officer, and the wedding was postponed for a year. Once Miss Ay’s obligations as Miss America and Mr. Sempier’s navy obligations were fulfilled, the couple married and later settled in Easttown, near Leopard, and sent their children to Easttown schools.

The township is also home to one of the top golfers of the past two decades. Jay Sigel, of Berwyn, turned in his eighth career win on the PGA Champions Tour at Kansas City, Missouri, in May of 2003. His first win came in 1994 at Ojai, California, the year he turned pro. Sigel was the country’s best amateur player in the early 1980s when he won back-to-back U.S. Amateur golf championships in 1982 and 1983. He also won three Mid-Amateur titles, was the 1979 British Amateur champion, played on nine U.S. Walker Cup teams, two as playing captain, and won the Pennsylvania state amateur championship eleven times.

Anthony J. “Skip” Minisi of Paoli, attorney, and long-time resident of Easttown township, also had, in his younger years, a significant football career. During his collegiate years between 1944 and 1947, Minisi was a left-handed passing All-American halfback. Though he spent most of his college career with the University of Pennsylvania’s Quakers, he was for one war-time year a Midshipmen with the U.S. Naval Academy He also played briefly with the New York Giants in the NFL before entering into law. He was inducted into the National Football Foundation College Hall of Fame in 1987. He presently serves on the Easttown Board of Supervisors; before that he was a member of the Tredyffrin/Easttown School Board.

An important amenity enjoyed by those living in Easttown township is Waynesborough Country Club which was organized in 1965. The Wayne mansion had been separated from its large tract of farm land and barn in 1926 when 300 acres were sold by William Wayne jr. to Robert Ligget. Up until World War II, Mr. Ligget kept a prize winning herd of Guernsey cattle there. The land, along today’s Route 252, ultimately became the site of the only country club in the township. In addition, Easttown township received a gift of the barn in 1980 and leased it to the country club for use by its maintenance and grounds department. The 1830s barn was restored by Waynesborough Country Club in 1999-2000, part of a project to upgrade its facilities prior to hosting the prestigious PGA golf tour event, the “Pennsylvania Classic,” held in September of 2000. A second Pennsylvania Classic was held at the club in 2002.

As the number of homes in the township rose, the desire for infrastructure and municipal services grew also. The need for waste disposal stood near the top of the list. A private disposal system, Devon Drainage Association, consisting of one line to service a few residents and the Devon Inn along the Darby creek lowlands, came into existence early in the century. It provided limited service to a limited area. When the Easttown Township School Board constructed the Devon grade school in 1957 and asked to be connected to this system, a new treatment plant was required. The cost increased subscribers bills by 50%. 

Some new construction, such as Devon Downs built in 1962 - 1964 was connected to the system. Ultimately, an Easttown Municipal Authority came into being which over the existing Devon Drainage in 1969 and financed escalting construction costs by borrowing. A regional authority began accepting Easttown waste in 1977, and the old Devon Drainage plant located at the end of Heatherwood road cul-de-sac was phased out and later demolished. A system was installed in 1978 to connect most housing units then existing in high density areas, while subsequent construction included provision for the service. The Municipal Authority expanded this service to the Leopard Lakes, Millbrook, and Fox Creek areas of the township in 1994. In 1970, there were 400 users. Twenty-five years later, Easttown had over 3000 customers, utilizing an approximate 70 miles of pipe.

“Project 2000,” another large investment in infrastructure commenced in 1996. The project addressed storm water drainage and roadway resurfacing as well as facility needs of police and administrative offices, library, and equipment for the police and public srvices to provide for Easttown’s future in the new century. A $5 million bond issue in early May 1996 provided the initial funding for the project. 

A new state law passed in 1988 mandated that municipalities provide for curbside pickup of recyclables and composting of leaves in oder to lessen the statewide need for landfills and Incinerators. The township appointed a Solid Waste Task Force to plan and implement compliance with the law. A local ordinance was enacted, a contract awarded to a single hauler, and curbside recycling and waste collection in Easttowncommenced July 1, 1990.

The township also prohibited outside burning including leaves, except for restricted burning of brush on specified days during each calendar year. Easttown has consistently recylced a higher proportion of its trash than any other municipality in Chester county.

American intervention in the Vietnamese war dragged on interminably in the 1960s and 1970s. While most Americans heard reports of the final collapse of South Vietnam on April, 30, 1975 and the large numbers fleeing that country only the most foresighted could have predicted what followed in Berwyn.

Trinity Presbyterian Church becam involved in an emergency situation unique in its history. A continuing effort began on April 28 when 56 refugees arrived from Vietnam. They were staff members of the Pearl S. Buck Foundation’s Saigon office. Pastor Robert W Bohl of Trinity was a member of the Foundation Board of Directors and Chairman of its Adoption Committee. Later 27 orphans arrived at Philadelphia airport bringing the total number of refugees to 83. Through the unceasing efforts of Dr. Bohl and church member resettlement volunteers over many weeks, all were found homes or adoptive parents. In recognition of their efforts, Freedoms Foundation honored Trinity Church and presented Dr. Bohl the Humanitarian Activities Award.

Footlighters Theatre, a community theater group which relocated from the Saturday Club in Wayne, took up residence at 58 Main avenue, Berwyn, in 1974 in the old Methodist church building. After renting the space for ten years, it became the permanent home of the Footlighters when they purchased the building from Trinity Presbyterian Church.

On May 22, 1991 a local landmark, St. Monica Roman Catholic Church, built between 1889 and 1893 was destroyed in a fire started by a roofing project. The parish rallied behind its pastor, the Rev. George C. Hagenbach, subscribed to a capital campaign drive, and erected a new edifice. Dedication of the new church building took place at ceremonies on September 12, 1993 attended by Anthony Cardinal Bevilacqua and other notables.

Easttown township administrative and police department offices, which had been quartered in one wing of the former Berwyn Elementary School since 1982, were moved to new quarters on March 24, 1999 at 566 Beaumont road in Devon. The location is a two-story converted stone barn at the Hilltop estate which was donated to the township by Dr. W.H. Sterg O’Dell and his wife Frances in 1996. 

Hilltop Park, a new township park constructed on the approximately 20-acre tract adjacent to the municipal offices, includes practice and regulation soccer fields, paved walking path, tot lot, picnic pavilion, parking area, new fencing, and landscaping. Dedication ceremonies at the park took place on May 8, 1999.

The Cassatt avenue bridge spanning the railroad tracks at the station in the center of Berwyn, opened in the late nineteenth century and closed in 1981, was reconstructed as a pedestrian walkway in a cooperative effort between SEPTA, the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation, the Federal Transit Administration, Chester County, and Easttown and Tredyffrin townships. The completed project was dedicated on May 13, 1999, amid light spring showers. The ceremony also included unveiling of the relocated World War I Veterans’ Memorial.

Seventy years after the first Route 30 construction through Berwyn, Easttown’s most heavily traveled street received a substantial update. In advance of the start of PennDot operations, work began September 18, 2000 with the water company replacing a 90-year old cement main under the middle of the roadway. Electric and gas and telephone utilities did their work during the summer of 2001. PennDot crews began their part of the project to completely rebuild the roadway on October 8, 2001, and, by the end of a year of torture, they had most of the final inch-and-a-half of asphalt on the road th:-ouglo Berwyn and Devon. The project was	completed in the spring of 2003, far ahead of deadline, and traffic picked up noticeably on our smooth, new main street.

A gathering was held on May 10, 2002 to mark the dedication and grand opening of	Easttown township’s Frank J.L. Johnson	Memorial Park, located on a four-acre tract purchased in 1989 in the northern section of Melgran Farms, at the south end of Bridge avenue in Berwyn. Tom Toscani, Chairman of the Park and Recreation board, presided over the event, which included Ms. Katie Johnson, daughter of the late Mr. Frank Johnson, who performed the ceremonial ribbon cutting.

The all new Easttown Library & Information center, located at 720 First Avenue in Berwyn opened for business on February 21, 2003. About 75 persons, including library staff, Friends of the Library, Easttown officials, and eager patrons gathered to celebrate. Hal Hurff, President of the Library Trustees, greeted the group and moderated the brief remarks of officials in attendance. The new facility replaced an older, smaller building on the same site which had been used since 1982. It was torn down to make way for the new 16,000 square-foot center which cost $4:2 million. For the approximately 13-month construction period, the library used temporary quarters in the Bronze building on Old Lancaster road in the east end of Berwyn.

The Acme supermarket in the Berwyn Shopping Center closed its doors for the last time on July 7, 2003, after serving customers at the location for nearly thirty-seven years. For the first time since the early 1920s residents of Easttown were without a local Acme (or American Store as they were called back then). On the last day, a group of residents gathered outside the door to reminiscence. Carol Butler, poet laureate of Berwyn, recited a poem she wrote to honor the store, its customers, and its employees. The group joined hands and sang “God Bless America"” and dispersed to their homes. So ended an era in Easttown.

However, before this era ended, our township officials reflected on the many years of change and progress in Easttown and suggested it would be appropriate to chronicle and celebrate this milestone, the long and interesting 300-year history of the township. To do this, Karl F. Klingelhoeffer, a long-time resident of the township and retired marketing executive, was asked to volunteer as chairman of the celebration. The not-for-profit Easttown Township Tricentennial Corporation was created, and an Executive Committee of volunteers was formed to execute the plan for the celebration. It included Herb Fry, Laura Caterson, Frank Castaldi, Steve Heumann, Marc Heppe, Jim Robbins, and Howard Fritz. This book is the result of their plan, as was the 2004 historic calendar which township residents received, a newspaper supplement, and many events which took place in the Tricentennial year.

So as we survey the three centuries of life in Easttown township recorded in this book, we can truly reflect that the challenges of the years were successfully met, and the quality of life of today’s residents is the highest. Looking to the future we can confidently affirm that Easttown township, although old in history is indeed young in spirit!

The Welsh Tract and Early Easttown Deeds

Only a few months after William Penn had received his grant for a colony in Pennsylvania from King Charles II, a committee representing a group of Welsh Quakers or Friends visited Penn in London. Arrangements were made at that time to reserve a tract of 40,000 acres, to be "layd out contiguously as one Barony" for their exclusive purchase and settlement, a tract where they hoped and expected to be able to preserve their traditions and language and customs. A survey was made in 1684 to establish the area to be included in this Welsh Tract, begun in April and completed before the end of the year. The tract extended from Merion Township in the east to Goshen and part of Westtown township on the west.
